title.rendered: MTRH CEO welcomes Pfizer delegation to strengthen regional specialized healthcare delivery

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Pfizer Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Dr. Albert Bourla has visited Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital (MTRH) as part of the pharmaceutical company’s ongoing engagement with Kenya’s healthcare sector.

During the visit, Dr. Bourla and the Pfizer leadership team held discussions with MTRH management and healthcare professionals on the hospital’s specialized services, particularly in oncology and pathology.

The discussions also explored opportunities for collaboration to strengthen access to quality healthcare and specialized medical services.

MTRH Chief Executive Officer Dr. Philip Kirwa welcomed the Pfizer delegation and highlighted the importance of partnerships with global pharmaceutical companies in supporting the hospital’s efforts to improve patient care.

Focus on cancer care and specialized services

The discussions placed particular attention on oncology, an area in which MTRH provides specialized services to patients from across Kenya and the wider region.

The hospital also shared information on its pathology services, which play an important role in diagnosing and managing cancer and other diseases.

Dr. Kirwa said collaboration with pharmaceutical companies could support efforts to expand access to advanced cancer care and strengthen the hospital’s capacity to respond to the growing demand for specialized services.

He also pointed to opportunities for cooperation beyond access to medicines.

These include medical research, healthcare innovation, professional capacity building and the adoption of advanced healthcare technologies.

Opportunities for research and innovation

The engagement also provided an opportunity for Pfizer and MTRH to explore areas where their respective expertise and resources could support healthcare development in Kenya.

Medical research emerged as a potential area of collaboration, with partnerships offering opportunities to strengthen evidence generation and support the development and adoption of innovative approaches to disease prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

Capacity building could also form part of future collaboration, particularly through opportunities that enhance the skills of healthcare professionals working in specialized fields.

MTRH has continued to develop its role as a referral and teaching institution, providing specialized medical services while supporting the training of healthcare professionals.

Engagement with international pharmaceutical companies could complement these efforts by creating opportunities for knowledge exchange and exposure to emerging healthcare technologies.

The visit comes as Kenya continues to strengthen partnerships across the healthcare sector to improve access to specialized treatment and essential medicines.

For MTRH, engagement with global pharmaceutical companies provides an opportunity to identify areas where external expertise and resources can support its clinical, research and training functions.

Dr. Bourla’s visit included meetings with hospital leaders and healthcare professionals, with discussions focusing on MTRH’s specialized services and potential areas of cooperation with Pfizer.

title.rendered: Alameda Healthcare Group expands regional footprint with new specialized clinic in Beni Suef

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

EGYPT—Alameda Healthcare Group has expanded its healthcare network in Egypt with the opening of a new As Salam International Hospitals Specialized Clinic in Beni Suef, increasing access to specialized medical services outside Greater Cairo.

Located at El Nasr Mall on Ahmed Oraby Street, the clinic houses more than 20 specialized clinics staffed by experienced medical consultants.

The facility is designed to give residents of Beni Suef access to specialist medical expertise closer to home.

The clinic was officially inaugurated at a ceremony attended by Eslam Edris, Group Chief Marketing Officer of Alameda Healthcare Group; Jasmine Singh, Chief Executive Officer of As Salam International Hospital Maadi; and Dr Raed Darwish, Chief Medical Officer of As Salam International Hospital Maadi. Governorate officials and physicians also attended the event.

Expanding beyond Greater Cairo

The Beni Suef opening forms part of Alameda Healthcare Group’s strategy to expand specialized healthcare services across Egypt.

The group is increasing its presence in cities outside Greater Cairo to bring specialist consultations and medical expertise closer to communities with growing healthcare needs.

With the addition of Beni Suef, Alameda Healthcare Group now operates seven specialized clinics in Cairo, Assiut, Suez, Ismailia, Zagazig, Mansoura and Beni Suef.

The group plans to open additional clinics in Tanta and Alexandria, which would increase its specialized clinic network to nine locations by the end of 2026.

The expanded network is expected to provide more than 100,000 outpatient consultations, further increasing the group’s capacity to serve patients nationwide.

Focus on accessible specialist services

Edris said the expansion into Beni Suef demonstrates the group’s commitment to making specialized healthcare more accessible to patients across Egypt.

“Access to leading medical expertise should not be limited by geography,” he said, adding that the new clinic would extend Alameda Healthcare Group’s standards of clinical care and patient experience to more communities.

The group also aims to strengthen continuity of care by connecting patients with specialist services within its broader healthcare network.

This approach is intended to make it easier for patients to receive consultations and follow up on their treatment without travelling long distances.

The Beni Suef clinic also expands As Salam International Hospitals’ reach into Upper Egypt.

It offers patients a range of medical specialties through a model that emphasizes convenient access, quality care and continuity of treatment.

The expansion comes as Alameda Healthcare Group continues to develop its network of healthcare facilities and specialized outpatient services across Egypt.

title.rendered: Sidra Medicine partners with Pearl International Hospital to expand access to cord blood banking in Qatar

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

QATAR—Sidra Medicine, a member of the Qatar Foundation, and The Pearl International Hospital have signed an agreement to give expectant parents access to cord blood banking services as part of their maternity care.

Under the agreement, parents receiving maternity services at The Pearl International Hospital can choose to preserve their baby’s umbilical cord blood with Sidra Medicine.

The hospital will coordinate the collection, while Sidra Medicine will process and store the samples at its specialized Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) facility, which houses Qatar’s only cord blood bank.

Prof. Khalid Fakhro, Chief Research Officer at Sidra Medicine, said the partnership would expand access to specialized cord blood and tissue banking services for families in Qatar.

He said the service would give parents the information and support they need to make informed decisions about preserving cord blood and other biological resources.

He added that the agreement reflects Sidra Medicine’s efforts to expand specialized healthcare services to patients and families across the country.

Dr. Cem Emir Guldogan, Chief Medical Officer at The Pearl International Hospital, said the hospital was proud to enter the agreement, describing it as an important step in its efforts to provide advanced medical care to the community.

He said the partnership marked a milestone in the hospital’s efforts to raise healthcare standards in Qatar.

According to Guldogan, The Pearl International Hospital combines medical expertise and innovative technologies with an environment designed to promote holistic well-being while providing compassionate care aligned with international best practices and community values.

Cord blood collection and potential uses

Healthcare professionals collect cord blood after clamping and cutting the umbilical cord. The procedure does not cause pain or pose additional risk to the mother or baby.

However, because collection can only take place immediately after birth, parents have a single opportunity to preserve the cord blood.

Cord blood contains hematopoietic stem cells that can be used to treat certain blood, immune and genetic disorders.

Researchers are also studying their potential applications in regenerative medicine, including possible treatments for conditions such as cerebral palsy, autism and type 1 diabetes.

Families enrolled in the service can potentially access their stored stem cells for future treatment of certain conditions affecting their child.

Depending on medical suitability and compatibility, the cells may also benefit other family members.

Local storage and specialized processing

Sidra Medicine’s GMP facility provides families with the option of storing cord blood in Qatar.

Local storage can support sample quality and facilitate access when the cells are medically required.

Beyond cord blood banking, the facility prepares bone marrow stem cells for transplantation and manufactures advanced cell and gene therapy products for pediatric patients at Sidra Medicine.

Where necessary, Sidra Medicine can also facilitate the transfer of stored stem cells to authorized centers in other countries, providing families with additional options for future clinical use.

title.rendered: M42 forms 10-year digital health and genomics alliance in Botswana

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—M42, a global healthcare company focused on artificial intelligence (AI), technology and genomics, has entered Africa through a 10-year strategic partnership with Botswana’s Ministry of Health.

The agreement, signed in Gaborone, marks M42’s first health systems partnership in Africa and expands the company’s international healthcare activities into the continent.

Digital health and precision medicine

Under the partnership, M42 will support Botswana’s efforts to transform its healthcare system through digital health, genomics, precision medicine and workforce development.

The company will also work with local and regional health professionals to strengthen technical capacity and expand access to advanced healthcare solutions.

The agreement was signed on behalf of the Government of Botswana by Acting Permanent Secretary Dr Tshepo Machacha, in the presence of Minister of Health Dr Stephen Modise and Kareem Shahin, Chief Executive Officer of M42’s Digital Health Solutions platform and Group Chief Digital Officer.

In addition, M42 and Mubadala Bio, a life sciences company, will work with Botswana to improve the supply of pharmaceuticals and medical equipment.

The initiative aims to establish a more reliable and sustainable medical supply chain, improve access to essential health products, and make procurement faster and more efficient.

Supporting universal health coverage

The partnership follows Botswana Parliament’s approval of the National Health Insurance Policy on August 19, 2026.

Presented by Dr Modise, the policy seeks to advance universal health coverage (UHC) by ensuring that citizens can access affordable and equitable healthcare regardless of their income or geographic location.

Against this backdrop, the partnership brings together Botswana’s healthcare priorities and M42’s capabilities in clinical care, genomics, digital health, AI and capacity building.

The collaboration will therefore support the Ministry of Health as it works to strengthen healthcare delivery and develop a more responsive health system.

Dr Modise said the agreement would strengthen Botswana’s health security and improve the resilience of its medical supply chains.

He added that the partnership would help ensure that patients do not go without medicines and medical products because of avoidable procurement and supply delays.

“Through this partnership, we are opening a reliable gateway to medicines, medical supplies, and health products whenever and wherever the country needs them,” he said.

M42 expands healthcare footprint in Africa

Dimitris Moulavasilis, Group Chief Executive of M42, said the company has been expanding its healthcare capabilities across the Global South, where countries can adopt digital and AI-enabled health systems without relying solely on legacy infrastructure.

He said the Botswana agreement provides an opportunity for M42 to deploy its capabilities in digital health transformation, genomics, precision medicine and capacity development in collaboration with the Ministry of Health.

Shahin said M42 was privileged to partner with Botswana as it works to transform its healthcare system.

He said the company supports the Ministry’s goal of building a system that citizens can rely on, with consistent access to medicines, effective technologies and healthcare services across communities.

He added that M42 would work with Botswana’s Ministry of Health and healthcare professionals to support the country’s healthcare priorities and improve the health and well-being of its population.

The partnership combines medical supply-chain development with collaboration in digital health, genomics, and precision medicine as Botswana advances its healthcare transformation agenda.

title.rendered: Sheikh Shakhbout Medical City launches multidisciplinary clinic to improve lupus care

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” custom_padding=”|||14px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content” custom_padding=”|||0px||” width=”100%” custom_margin=”|||-17px||”]

UAE— Sheikh Shakhbout Medical City (SSMC), a subsidiary of PureHealth, has launched an integrated multidisciplinary Lupus Clinic to provide coordinated, patient-centred care for people living with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

The clinic brings together rheumatologists, nephrologists, dermatologists, neurologists, haematologists and other specialists so patients can receive comprehensive assessments and coordinated treatment during a single visit.

This approach reduces the need for multiple referrals and appointments across different specialties, which can otherwise take weeks or months.

In addition, patients can access pharmacy services, psychological support and other specialised services as part of the coordinated care model.

The multidisciplinary team works together to develop an individualised treatment plan based on each patient’s needs.

Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease that can affect several organs, including the joints, skin, kidneys, brain and cardiovascular system.

It predominantly affects women aged 15 to 45, with the World Lupus Federation estimating that women account for approximately 90% of people living with the disease.

A 2023 study estimated that about 16,500 people in the UAE live with lupus.

Because the disease can affect different organs and often presents symptoms similar to other conditions, patients may experience delays in diagnosis and treatment.

Supporting women through pregnancy

The clinic also provides specialised support for women with lupus who are planning to have children.

Through collaboration between rheumatology, obstetrics and haematology teams, patients can receive pregnancy planning, maternal-foetal monitoring and blood-clot management.

This coordinated approach allows specialists to monitor disease activity and potential complications throughout pregnancy while ensuring that treatment decisions account for both maternal and fetal health.

Dr Abdulqader Almessabi, Chief Medical Officer at SSMC, said lupus often requires lifelong care from multiple specialists.

“At SSMC, our goal is to provide a coordinated model that puts the patient at the centre of every decision,” he said.

He added that the clinic demonstrates SSMC’s commitment to integrated care by improving collaboration among specialists and enabling patients to receive faster, more personalised treatment.

Earlier diagnosis and coordinated treatment

Lupus can affect multiple organs and may require patients to consult several specialists during their care journey.

Doctors may also need to conduct extensive investigations, including specialised blood tests and, in some cases, skin or kidney biopsies, to confirm a diagnosis.

By bringing specialists together, the clinic aims to facilitate timely diagnosis and early intervention, potentially reducing the risk of long-term organ damage and disease progression.

Dr Mumtaz Khan, Consultant and Chair of the Rheumatology Division at SSMC, said many people with lupus spend years seeking a diagnosis and coordinated treatment.

He said the combined clinic allows patients to meet rheumatologists, dermatologists, nephrologists, haematologists and neurologists together during the same visit.

This enables specialists to agree on a unified approach to diagnosis and treatment and make faster, more informed decisions.

The Lupus Clinic forms part of SSMC’s efforts to expand specialised multidisciplinary services for people with complex autoimmune diseases and strengthen integrated lupus care in Abu Dhabi and the wider region through research, education and clinical excellence.

title.rendered: Gauteng receives 28,593 Lenacapavir packs as demand for HIV prevention rises

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

SOUTH AFRICA—The Gauteng Department of Health (GDoH) has received an additional 28,593 Lenacapavir initiation packs as the province expands access to the six-monthly, long-acting injection for HIV prevention.

The department said it is distributing the new stock to 133 participating healthcare facilities across Gauteng.

The replenishment will restore supplies at facilities in Tshwane, Johannesburg, and Sedibeng that experienced temporary shortages after demand exceeded initial projections following the programme’s rollout in June 2026.

Many facilities across the province still have stock available, while the latest consignment brings the total number of initiation packs received by Gauteng to 57,231 across three batches.

By the end of July 2026, healthcare providers had initiated 17,937 eligible clients on Lenacapavir, reflecting strong demand for the HIV prevention option.

Gauteng has been allocated enough stock to initiate 114,160 eligible clients between June 2026 and March 2027, with additional supplies scheduled for quarterly delivery.

Strong demand for HIV prevention

Gauteng MEC for Health and Wellness Faith Mazibuko said the strong public response showed that more residents were taking proactive steps to prevent HIV infection.

“The overwhelming demand for Lenacapavir is a positive sign that more people are embracing HIV prevention services and taking charge of their health,” Mazibuko said.

She added that the response highlighted the need for prevention options that are convenient, effective and suited to people’s lifestyles and circumstances.

The department said the temporary shortages resulted from demand exceeding initial estimates.

It acknowledged the frustration experienced by some clients and said it was working to restore supplies so eligible people can access Lenacapavir at any of the 133 participating facilities.

Lenacapavir for prevention, not treatment

The GDoH also reminded the public that Lenacapavir is intended to prevent HIV and is not a treatment for people already living with the virus.

Individuals must undergo HIV testing before receiving the injection to confirm their eligibility.

Healthcare workers have also continued educating clients about the eligibility requirements after some people living with HIV requested the injection.

Although Lenacapavir is highly effective at preventing HIV infection, it does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or unplanned pregnancies.

The department therefore encouraged residents to continue using condoms and undergo regular HIV and STI screening, which remain available free of charge at public healthcare facilities across Gauteng.

Strengthening programme implementation

To improve access, the department has strengthened provincial and district stock-monitoring systems and expanded training for healthcare workers, pharmacists, programme managers and data personnel.

It also conducts weekly monitoring of programme implementation, clinical guidelines and reporting systems, while community engagement and demand-creation activities continue to support uptake.

Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) remains available as another HIV prevention option.

The department said Lenacapavir complements rather than replaces existing prevention methods.

Clients who receive Lenacapavir must attend scheduled follow-up appointments.

They return one month after initiation and every six months thereafter for subsequent injections, HIV retesting, clinical monitoring and support.

title.rendered: Aga Khan University Hospital performs region’s first robotic-assisted gallbladder surgery

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Aga Khan University Hospital, Nairobi (AKUH,N) has performed the region’s first robotic-assisted gallbladder removal surgery, marking a significant milestone in the adoption of advanced minimally invasive surgical care in Kenya.

The procedure, medically known as robotic-assisted laparoscopic cholecystectomy, combines surgical expertise with robotic technology to enhance precision, visualisation and control during an operation.

Unlike conventional open surgery, the technique allows surgeons to perform the procedure through small incisions using specialised instruments controlled from a surgical console.

Enhanced precision and visualisation

Dr Abdulkarim Abdalla, Chair of the Hospital’s Department of Surgery, said robotic-assisted surgery builds on the established benefits of conventional keyhole surgery while giving surgeons greater control over surgical instruments.

According to Abdalla, the technology provides a three-dimensional view of the surgical field, allowing surgeons to see anatomical structures more clearly during the procedure.

It also gives them greater flexibility when operating in areas that can be difficult to access or visualise using conventional laparoscopic techniques.

The robotic system does not operate independently. Instead, surgeons control the camera and instruments from a specialised console, directing every movement throughout the procedure.

“Robotic-assisted surgery builds on the benefits of conventional keyhole surgery by providing surgeons with a three-dimensional view of the surgical field, greater flexibility of movement, and improved access to areas that can be difficult to visualise using traditional techniques,” Abdalla said.

The robotic instruments also offer a wider range of movement and closely replicate the movements of the human hand.

As a result, surgeons can perform delicate surgical tasks with greater precision and control.

Potential benefits for patients

Robotic-assisted surgery retains many of the benefits associated with minimally invasive procedures.

These include smaller surgical incisions, reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stays and faster recovery compared with traditional open surgery.

The technology may also improve the surgeon’s working environment.

Because surgeons operate while seated at a specialised console, the system can potentially reduce physical fatigue during lengthy procedures.

At the same time, enhanced visualisation and instrument flexibility can support more complex surgical tasks.

The successful procedure demonstrates the hospital’s growing use of advanced surgical technologies to expand minimally invasive treatment options for patients in Kenya and the wider region.

Expanding surgical innovation

Rashid Khalani, Chief Executive Officer of AKUH,N, said the milestone builds on the hospital’s history of introducing new healthcare technologies and services in Kenya and across the region.

“Since our inception, Aga Khan University Hospital has built a tradition of introducing many healthcare firsts for Kenya and the region,” Khalani said. “This latest milestone continues that legacy. We invest in innovation because it enables safer, precise and evidence-based care for our patients.”

He added that the hospital plans to expand access to robotic-assisted surgery while strengthening surgical excellence, research and training across the region.

The initiative is expected to support the development of specialised surgical expertise and provide additional opportunities for clinicians to gain experience with advanced robotic technologies.

title.rendered: Kenya advocates for more investment in Africa’s health self-reliance

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Kenya has called on African countries to turn the continent’s health agenda into concrete investments, measurable results and stronger systems that reduce reliance on external support.

Health Cabinet Secretary Hon. Aden Duale made the call during a plenary session of the 76th WHO Regional Committee for Africa, where Member States discussed A New Era of Health for Africa: United Action for Vision 2035.

WHO Regional Director for Africa Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi presented the strategy during a session chaired by Ethiopia’s Minister for Health, Dr. Mekdes Daba.

Kenya endorsed the strategy, saying it aligns with ongoing efforts to develop a resilient, accessible and sustainable health system.

However, CS Duale said Africa must translate its commitment to health self-reliance into action, focusing on sustainable health financing, local manufacturing and digital transformation.

On health financing, he urged African governments to strengthen domestic resource mobilisation and increase fiscal allocations to health.

He said countries cannot continue to depend heavily on external financing to sustain essential health services.

He highlighted Kenya’s Taifa Care programme under the Social Health Authority, which has enrolled more than 32 million people and is strengthening domestic financing for primary healthcare.

CS Duale also called on the WHO Regional Office for Africa to help countries develop stronger health investment cases and facilitate joint engagements between Health and Finance Ministers to secure sustainable domestic funding.

Expanding local pharmaceutical manufacturing

On local manufacturing, CS Duale highlighted Kenya’s ratification of the treaty establishing the African Medicines Agency and encouraged other Member States to accelerate the ratification process.

He said a stronger continental regulatory framework, combined with pooled procurement and joint regulatory approvals, would create predictable demand for locally manufactured medicines and expand opportunities for African pharmaceutical companies.

“Health product sovereignty will ultimately be built through procurement and sustained demand, not declarations alone,” he said.

Advancing digital health

Kenya also outlined progress in digital health, including the development of an integrated national architecture linking health facilities, claims management systems and national health registries.

These digital platforms are also supporting community-level healthcare through more than 107,000 Community Health Promoters.

In addition, Kenya backed the establishment of a regional health data hub based on interoperable standards, strong data governance and systems owned and trusted by Member States.

The proposed approach would strengthen the continent’s ability to manage and protect its health data.

CS Duale reaffirmed Kenya’s commitment to working with the WHO Regional Director and other Member States to implement the regional strategy and strengthen Africa’s health systems.

Kenya’s delegation included Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union H.E. Galma Boru; Director-General for Health Dr. Patrick Amoth; Digital Health Agency CEO Eng. Anthony Lenaiyara; and Director of Health Sector Coordination and Intergovernmental Relations Dr. Omar Albush.

title.rendered: WHO African Region Ministers convene in Ethiopia to shape health agenda

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

ETHIOPIA— Ministers of health from the 47 Member States of the World Health Organization (WHO) African Region have opened the 76th session of the WHO Regional Committee for Africa in Addis Ababa, beginning three days of discussions on policies and priorities that will shape the region’s health agenda.

The Regional Committee, the WHO African Region’s highest decision-making body, brings together health ministers, senior government officials, development partners and technical experts.

During the session, participants are reviewing progress, addressing emerging health challenges and considering strategies to strengthen health systems and improve health outcomes across the continent.

Opening the session, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie called for stronger regional cooperation and sustained investment in resilient health systems to improve health and support Africa’s development.

“Africa’s next health chapter must be defined by ownership over dependency, integration over fragmentation and practical action over words,” President Taye said. “Let us act not only with declarations, but with firm commitment and measurable actions.”

Ethiopia calls for resilient health systems

Ethiopian Minister of Health Dr Mekdes Daba urged countries to build sustainable health systems that can respond to the region’s changing needs.

She highlighted persistent inequalities, limited resources, emerging technologies, climate-related challenges, demographic shifts and increasingly complex health emergencies as major pressures on African health systems.

“If we act in solidarity, invest with purpose, and innovate with equity at the centre, we can build an Africa that is healthier, more resilient, more self-reliant and better prepared to shape its future,” Dr Daba said.

WHO Regional Director for Africa Dr Mohamed Janabi said the meeting demonstrates Member States’ shared commitment to stronger, more resilient and self-reliant health systems through collective action and African-led solutions.

He said Addis Ababa provided an appropriate setting for the meeting because the city hosts the African Union and has long served as a centre for continental diplomacy and cooperation.

“The decisions we take this week will shape policies, guide investments and influence future generations,” Dr Janabi said, urging countries to remain ambitious, practical and accountable.

Health financing, workforce and child development

Among the key agenda items is a strategy to strengthen sustainable health financing across the region.

Ministers will also consider the Africa Health Workforce Agenda 2026–2035, which aims to help countries train, employ and retain more health workers.

In addition, delegates will discuss a regional strategy focused on giving children the best possible start in life by increasing investment in early childhood development.

Strengthening health security and data

Ministers will consider proposals to improve the regulation of medical products and strengthen health security and emergency preparedness.

The discussions come as African countries continue to face frequent public health emergencies.

Against the backdrop of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ebola response, ministers will review a framework for strengthening national emergency medical teams.

The framework aims to help countries respond more quickly and effectively to outbreaks, disasters and other emergencies.

The Committee will also consider measures to protect Africa’s progress against polio by maintaining surveillance systems, laboratories, skilled personnel and emergency response capabilities developed through decades of eradication efforts.

Furthermore, delegates will examine a new Regional Health Data Hub to help countries detect health threats earlier, allocate resources more effectively and make better-informed decisions.

The meeting will also consider A New Era of Health for Africa: United Action for Vision 2035, a long-term framework focused on primary health care, resilient health systems, sustainable financing, digital transformation and greater country ownership.

The resolutions adopted during the session will guide national policies, regional cooperation and WHO support to Member States over the coming year.

title.rendered: UAE hospitals expand AI and connected technologies to transform patient care

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—Healthcare providers across the United Arab Emirates are expanding the use of artificial intelligence (AI), predictive algorithms, and connected medical devices to improve care in hospitals across all seven emirates.

Deployments reported in August 2026 are focusing on diagnostic accuracy, continuous patient monitoring, emergency response and access to specialist care.

Hospitals are using these technologies in areas including mammography, stroke treatment, cancer care, sepsis detection, cardiology, neonatal services and emergency triage.

At the same time, connected medical equipment can transfer clinical data directly to monitoring centres and electronic health records.

Abu Dhabi expands AI in diagnostics and critical care

In Abu Dhabi, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi uses Transpara software to analyse digital mammograms and identify suspicious areas before clinicians review the images.

The hospital also uses ARTIS Icono 3D imaging to support urgent stroke interventions, while intelligent radiotherapy software helps adjust cancer treatment doses during care.

Meanwhile, Sheikh Shakhbout Medical City has equipped smart inpatient rooms with contactless sensors that monitor vital signs and assess patients’ risk of falling.

Wireless mobiCARE devices also provide continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring and transmit patient data to hospital control rooms.

Similarly, Sheikh Khalifa Medical City and Al Ain Hospital use algorithms and alert systems to identify patients at risk of sepsis and septic shock.

By detecting warning signs early, the systems give clinical teams additional time to begin treatment.

Tawam Hospital has also introduced Histotripsy technology for treating liver tumours. The technology uses focused acoustic waves to target and destroy tissue without conventional invasive surgery.

Dubai and Sharjah strengthen connected monitoring

In Dubai, Rashid Hospital and Dubai Hospital operate wireless patient-monitoring networks alongside intelligent emergency-department triage systems.

These technologies help staff prioritise critically ill patients and direct them to appropriate care more quickly.

At Al Jalila Children’s Speciality Hospital, algorithm-assisted digital electroencephalogram (EEG) equipment helps identify patterns associated with epileptic seizures and convulsions before they occur.

The technology therefore extends predictive monitoring into paediatric neurological care.

In Sharjah, healthcare facilities are deploying computer-vision systems and smart clinical-monitoring technologies in operating theatres and intensive care units.

Khorfakkan Hospital and Kalba Hospital also use wireless foetal-monitoring equipment and digital wristbands that track patients’ vital signs.

Meanwhile, Dibba Al Hisn Specialised Health Centre uses AI-powered cameras to analyse retinal images and support earlier detection of diabetes-related complications.

Remote diagnostics extend specialist access

Healthcare providers are also using connected diagnostic technologies to extend specialist services to patients in remote areas.

Al Dhafra Hospitals in Madinat Zayed, Ghayathi and Al Mirfa use connected diagnostic kits that allow healthcare professionals to conduct examinations remotely.

The devices transmit live audio and video to consultants, enabling specialists to support patients beyond major urban hospitals.

Similarly, Masfout Hospital uses digital diagnostic equipment to support telemedicine services in mountainous areas of Ajman.

Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Hospital combines digital screening technologies with sensor-equipped smart beds designed to help reduce the risk of pressure injuries.

title.rendered: Minister of Economy visits Thumbay Medicity to support health and longevity tourism goals

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—His Excellency Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri, Minister of Economy and Tourism, has visited Thumbay Medicity in Ajman, highlighting the growing role of healthcare, medical education, and health tourism in the UAE’s diversified, knowledge-based economy.

Dr. Thumbay Moideen, Founder and President of Thumbay Group, received H.E. Bin Touq alongside Akbar Moideen Thumbay, Vice President of the Healthcare Division, and senior leaders from the Group’s academic and clinical institutions.

Focus on Health and Longevity Tourism

During the visit, H.E. Bin Touq said medical and longevity tourism represent rapidly expanding sectors worldwide.

He noted that the UAE continues to strengthen its infrastructure and capabilities to attract international patients and visitors while enhancing the competitiveness of its tourism industry.

According to the Minister, these efforts support the UAE’s ambition to become a leading global hub for advanced and sustainable health and wellness services.

He also highlighted Thumbay Group’s contribution to strengthening the country’s position in medical and longevity tourism.

The Group has established a network that attracts students from more than 111 countries and patients from across the region.

H.E. Bin Touq said institutions such as Thumbay Medicity help create specialized healthcare and educational experiences while attracting international talent, encouraging innovation and delivering services that meet international standards.

Integrated Healthcare and Education Model

H.E. Bin Touq toured Gulf Medical University (GMU), the region’s leading private medical university, as well as Thumbay Medicity’s academic hospitals, including Thumbay University Hospital, Thumbay Dental Hospital and Thumbay Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Hospital.

During the tour, Group representatives presented Thumbay Medicity’s integrated model, which brings education, patient care and research together within the same healthcare ecosystem.

They also highlighted GMU’s development since its establishment in 1998 and its growing international student community.

Today, GMU attracts students from more than 111 countries, giving it one of the most internationally diverse student bodies among medical universities worldwide.

The discussions also examined how private healthcare and academic institutions contribute to the national economy and support the UAE’s emergence as a destination for health and wellness tourism.

Participants further explored the role of institutions such as Thumbay Medicity in attracting international patients, students and investment.

Thumbay Group’s Vision

Commenting on the visit, Dr. Thumbay Moideen said it was a privilege to welcome H.E. Bin Touq to Thumbay Medicity.

“When we established Gulf Medical University in 1998, we set out to build institutions that would serve the UAE for generations—educating doctors, healing patients and advancing research from the UAE to the world,” he said.

He added that the Minister’s visit recognized the progress of that vision and the growing contribution of healthcare and medical education to the UAE’s tourism ambitions.

He reaffirmed the Group’s commitment to supporting the country’s goal of becoming a global hub for health tourism and knowledge-based industries.

Research and Innovation

The visit concluded with H.E. Bin Touq touring Thumbay Medicity’s research and innovation facilities, where he reviewed key projects and initiatives.

He also met faculty members, clinicians and students, who shared their experiences and perspectives on the Medicity’s educational and research environment.

title.rendered: Aga Khan University Hospital deploys radiation dose monitoring technology to enhance patient safety

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Aga Khan University Hospital, Nairobi (AKUH, N) has implemented an advanced radiation dose management system designed to reduce patients’ exposure to ionising radiation while maintaining diagnostic image quality.

The technology, DoseMonitor®, connects with the hospital’s imaging equipment to automatically capture data on the amount of radiation used during procedures.

It analyses the data, compares radiation doses with international safety benchmarks and alerts clinical teams when further review or adjustment may be required.

Radiological procedures, including X-rays, computed tomography (CT) scans, mammograms, fluoroscopy, SPECT-CT, PET-CT, and cardiac catheterisation, are essential for diagnosing and managing a wide range of conditions.

However, because these procedures involve varying levels of ionising radiation, healthcare providers must carefully balance diagnostic requirements with radiation safety.

Dr Khalid Makhdomi, Chair of the Department of Radiology at AKUH,N, said DoseMonitor® incorporates internationally recognised radiation dose reference levels and benchmarks based on global best practices.

According to him, the system provides clinicians with real-time information that supports safer and more informed imaging decisions.

He added that the technology would enable more personalised imaging decisions while helping clinicians manage radiation exposure more effectively.

Supporting paediatric imaging

Dr Bernadette Muthee, a paediatric radiologist at AKUH,N, said DoseMonitor® is particularly valuable in paediatric imaging, where limiting radiation exposure is a key priority.

Meanwhile, AKUH,N CEO Rashid Khalani described the technology’s introduction as an important milestone in the hospital’s efforts to place patient safety at the centre of care.

“Patients should feel empowered to ask how their radiation exposure is being monitored and managed,” Khalani said.

He added that DoseMonitor® provides clinicians with tools to monitor exposure more consistently and effectively.

Mike Battin, COO of PACSHEALTH, LLC, the developer and distributor of DoseMonitor®, said innovative technologies that improve patient care remain central to the company’s work.

He said the company was pleased to add AKUH,N to its global portfolio of DoseMonitor® customers and congratulated the hospital on becoming the first site in the region to undertake dedicated patient radiation dose monitoring.

Kaye Bonython, Managing Director for PACSHealth Ltd UK/EMEA, said the company was pleased to work with AKUH,N to implement its patient monitoring software.

She noted that clinicians were already using the platform to manage radiation doses, save staff time when assessing dose parameters and support imaging for adults, children and expectant mothers.

Advancing local radiation research

Beyond clinical care, the system could generate data to support research into radiation exposure among African populations.

Many international radiation reference levels rely on data from Europe and North America, where patient demographics, body composition, disease patterns and healthcare environments can differ from those in Africa.

Stacy Achoki, Radiation Safety Officer at AKUH, N, said data generated through DoseMonitor could help the hospital contribute to developing locally relevant radiation reference levels for African populations.

She added that such research could inform future policy, strengthen radiation protection practices and support improved patient care standards across the continent.

AKUH, N said the deployment makes it the first hospital in Africa to implement DoseMonitor, reinforcing its focus on advanced imaging technology, patient safety and clinical care.

title.rendered: Liberia opens new Koon’s Town primary healthcare clinic in rural Montserrado

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

LIBERIA—The Ministry of Health, in partnership with development organizations, has officially opened the newly constructed Koon’s Town Primary Health Care Clinic in Todee District, rural Montserrado County, to improve access to essential healthcare services for surrounding communities.

The opening ceremony brought together representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO), the French Development Agency, the Government of France, Action Against Hunger, county authorities, community and religious leaders, traditional midwives, healthcare workers, and residents.

Speaking at the ceremony, Minister of Health Dr. Louise M. Kpoto thanked the Government of France, the French Development Agency, and Action Against Hunger for supporting Liberia’s healthcare system.

She also commended healthcare workers serving Koon’s Town and surrounding communities.

The Minister said the government would ensure that the clinic receives an ambulance. She noted that the government is procuring 15 ambulances as part of efforts to strengthen emergency medical services.

French support for health infrastructure

French Ambassador to Liberia Isabelle Le Guellec said the facility demonstrates France’s commitment to helping Liberia strengthen its national health system.

France and its partners supported the construction and equipping of the clinic before handing it over to the Government of Liberia, the Ministry of Health, and the County Health Team.

Le Guellec urged national and local authorities, healthcare workers, and community members to maintain the facility and ensure its continued delivery of quality care.

Action Against Hunger Country Director Sukhdev Sharma described the clinic as the result of collaboration among government institutions, development partners, healthcare workers, local leaders, and the community.

He thanked the French Development Agency and the Ministry of Health for their support throughout the project.

WHO and other participating partners also reaffirmed their commitment to working with the Ministry of Health to expand access to quality healthcare across Liberia.

Replacement of deteriorated facility

Action Against Hunger constructed the new clinic in partnership with the Government of France and the French Development Agency through the BEHOL Project.

The previous facility had deteriorated significantly and no longer met minimum standards for structural safety or effective service delivery.

Following an assessment by the Ministry of Health and its partners, authorities recommended replacing the outdated structure with a new Level 2 Primary Health Care facility to provide safer and more reliable services.

Koon’s Town Clinic was originally built in 2008 by the Liberia Agency for Community Empowerment as an emergency facility.

It serves 64 catchment communities and a population of 6,970 people, including 10 communities within a 5-kilometre radius and 54 located farther away.

The clinic provides reproductive, maternal, neonatal, and child health services, including antenatal care, labour and delivery, immunization, HIV counselling and testing, mental health support, and nutrition counselling.

The new facility includes medical equipment and furniture for essential service areas, including the Maternal and Child Health Unit.

It also has a 17.6-kilowatt solar power system, a waste management system, and other infrastructure designed to support safe and continuous healthcare delivery.

title.rendered: Uganda Martyrs Hospital Ibanda commissions new medical laboratory to expand diagnostic services

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UGANDA—Uganda Martyrs Hospital Ibanda has commissioned a modern medical laboratory to expand diagnostic services and reduce the need to refer patients’ samples to facilities in Mbarara for specialized testing.

The Archbishop of Mbarara Archdiocese, Rev. Lambert Bainomugisha, officially commissioned the facility on Friday during a ceremony attended by Christine Nimwesiga, Registrar of the Uganda Nurses and Midwives Council.

The new laboratory will allow the hospital to perform a wider range of diagnostic tests on-site.

As a result, clinicians are expected to receive test results more quickly, enabling them to make faster decisions about patient treatment.

Speaking during the ceremony, the hospital’s Medical Director, Dr. Gothaldo Tumubugane, said the facility addresses a longstanding gap in the hospital’s laboratory capacity.

“The hospital has been facing challenges in carrying out some laboratory tests, and we have been referring samples to other facilities in Mbarara. This has been inconveniencing our patients and delaying treatment. With this new laboratory, we are confident that the quality and efficiency of our laboratory services will greatly improve,” Tumubugane said.

Previously, patients requiring tests unavailable at the hospital had to wait while their samples were transported to facilities in Mbarara.

The additional transportation and processing time could delay diagnosis and the start of treatment.

Nursing and midwifery graduates enter workforce

The laboratory commissioning coincided with the graduation of more than 200 students from Ibanda School of Nursing and Midwifery.

The graduates completed certificate and diploma programmes in nursing and midwifery and are now joining Uganda’s healthcare workforce.

Their entry comes as health facilities continue to require qualified professionals to provide patient care and support growing healthcare needs.

As the chief guest, Nimwesiga urged the graduates to uphold professional standards, integrity, and compassion throughout their careers.

“Integrity is the foundation of the nursing profession. Wherever you go to serve, let honesty, discipline and compassion define your work,”she said.

“At the same time, embrace lifelong learning because healthcare continues to evolve, and you must keep improving your knowledge and skills,”

She also encouraged the graduates to pursue continuous professional development and recognise that their responsibilities extend beyond technical expertise to include ethical and compassionate patient care.

Archbishop urges graduates to prioritise patients

In his pastoral message, Archbishop Bainomugisha reminded the graduates that nursing requires dedication and a willingness to put patients’ needs before personal comfort.

“Nursing is not just a profession; it is a vocation. Be resilient, embrace self-denial, and be willing to forego personal comfort in order to serve those in need. The people you care for are depending on your dedication and compassion,” Bainomugisha said.

He urged the graduates to uphold the values of the nursing and midwifery professions and serve as ambassadors of quality healthcare wherever they are deployed.

Hospital officials said the new laboratory will strengthen access to diagnostic services in Ibanda and surrounding areas by bringing more testing closer to patients and reducing delays associated with referring samples to other facilities.

title.rendered: PureHealth launches Healthy Horizons to advance senior care in Abu Dhabi

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—PureHealth has partnered with the Family Development Foundation (FDF) to launch Healthy Horizons, a community outreach programme aimed at improving preventive care, healthy ageing and digital health access for Emirati senior citizens in Abu Dhabi.

The initiative is being delivered with the Emirates Foundation, Active Abu Dhabi, and PureHealth entities, including SEHA, SEHA Clinics, Sheikh Shakhbout Medical City (SSMC), and SAKINA.

It combines specialist-led workshops, free health screenings and guided physical activities to help identify health risks early, support timely intervention and improve continuity of care.

Participants also receive assistance with registering for the Pura app, PureHealth’s AI-powered health companion, enabling them to access digital health services and remain connected with their care teams.

Focus on key health needs

Healthy Horizons addresses several health priorities among older adults, including geriatric medicine, chronic disease management, vision health, sleep quality and mental wellbeing.

In addition to receiving practical health advice, participants are connected with PureHealth’s clinical network for continued support after the community sessions.

Fatima Aziz Al Marzouqi, Social Clubs Officer at Barakat Al Dar, part of the Family Development Foundation, said the organisation is committed to programmes that promote the physical and mental wellbeing of senior citizens and residents.

She added that Healthy Horizons can improve access to high-quality healthcare by making services more responsive to individual needs.

According to Al Marzouqi, Barakat Al Dar Social Club also helps senior citizens lead more active and engaged lives by strengthening family relationships and community connections.

She said these efforts reflect the foundation’s commitment to protecting the dignity of older adults, improving their wellbeing and enabling them to remain active members of society.

Leya Al Damani, Chief Sustainability Officer at PureHealth, said sustainable healthcare extends beyond treating illness to include early intervention, community resilience and helping older adults remain active in society.

She added that connecting community outreach with specialist healthcare and digital services across PureHealth’s network would support a model focused on measurable social impact and long-term health outcomes.

Community-based delivery

PureHealth has already begun conducting free preventive screenings and helping senior citizens access the Pura digital health platform.

Meanwhile, 54 trained volunteers from PureHeroes, a national healthcare volunteering platform launched by the Emirates Foundation and PureHealth, have contributed more than 270 service hours to the programme.

The volunteers support community health activities and help establish a structured model that can be expanded to reach more older adults.

Healthy Horizons also forms part of PureHealth’s wider longevity and senior health strategy.

It complements dedicated geriatric services such as the Barakatna Clinic, which SSMC launched in December 2025 in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Community Development and the Family Development Foundation.

Supporting national healthy-ageing goals

The programme aligns with the UAE’s National Policy for Senior Citizens and supports the objectives of the Centennial Plan 2071 by promoting preventive healthcare, digital readiness and sustainable community wellbeing.

It also supports the Barakatna initiative launched by UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to improve the wellbeing and quality of life of senior citizens through Abu Dhabi’s community care system.

Healthy Horizons will operate as a recurring outreach programme, with plans to expand into additional communities, increase preventive screening coverage and strengthen digital follow-up for participating senior citizens.

title.rendered: GCC Aesthetic Medicine training evolves as demand for clinical expertise grows

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”]

UAE—Aesthetic medicine in the Gulf is entering a more mature phase as the rapid growth of clinics, patient demand, and non-surgical cosmetic procedures shifts attention towards another critical area: the training and clinical competence of healthcare professionals.

Across Dubai, Doha, Riyadh, Muscat and other Gulf cities, physicians, dentists, nurses and other eligible healthcare professionals are encountering an increasingly diverse range of aesthetic treatments.

However, mastering individual techniques is only one part of the challenge.

As the sector evolves, practitioners also need strong knowledge of anatomy, patient assessment, treatment planning, complication prevention and clinical decision-making.

A diverse but connected regional market

The Gulf is not a single aesthetic medicine market.

Dubai has emerged as an internationally recognised destination for aesthetic procedures, supported by a large private healthcare sector and diverse international workforce.

Doha is continuing to expand its healthcare and medical education ecosystem, while Saudi Arabia has a large and rapidly developing healthcare market.

Despite these differences, the markets share several trends.

Patients have greater access to information, social media can rapidly popularise treatment trends, and practitioners are increasingly exposed to techniques and technologies developed in other parts of the world.

However, the popularity of a procedure can sometimes grow faster than the clinical expertise needed to deliver it safely and appropriately.

As a result, aesthetic medicine education in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) is increasingly moving beyond isolated demonstrations towards broader clinical training.

Moving beyond technique

Aesthetic procedures may appear relatively simple, but they can require considerable clinical knowledge.

Even a short injectable treatment can involve an understanding of facial anatomy, vascular structures, product characteristics, injection depth, patient selection, contraindications and potential complications.

Consequently, technical ability cannot be separated from clinical judgment.

Practitioners must understand not only how to perform a procedure but also when it is appropriate, which patients are suitable and how to respond when complications occur.

Online education has made medical knowledge more accessible, allowing healthcare professionals across the Gulf to study theory and observe procedures without travelling abroad.

However, procedural medicine presents an important limitation: watching a procedure does not necessarily prepare a practitioner to perform it independently.

Supervised practical training can help bridge this gap.

Hands-on aesthetic medicine education allows healthcare professionals to develop procedural skills while applying anatomical and clinical knowledge under supervision.

Online and in-person education can therefore complement rather than replace each other.

Practitioners can study theoretical concepts remotely, while procedural competencies can benefit from supervised practical experience.

Dubai and Doha expand regional training access

Dubai’s international healthcare workforce gives the city a distinctive position within the regional aesthetics sector.

Practitioners trained under different medical systems often work within the same market, creating opportunities for knowledge exchange while also increasing the need for common approaches to patient assessment, safety and complication management.

Dubai’s accessibility also allows healthcare professionals from neighbouring countries to attend regional training without travelling to Europe or North America.

A similar development is taking place in Qatar.

As Doha’s healthcare and professional education ecosystem expands, practitioners have increasing opportunities to access specialised training closer to their workplaces.

The Canadian Board of Aesthetic Medicine (CBAM), for example, has extended aspects of its medical aesthetics education activities into the GCC.

This reflects a broader shift in which international medical education organisations are increasingly bringing professional training into the region rather than requiring Gulf-based practitioners to travel overseas.

Saudi Arabia could further accelerate this trend as its healthcare sector expands and demand for specialised professional education increases.

Aesthetic medicine broadens its scope

The changing educational landscape also reflects the growing diversity of aesthetic medicine itself.

Injectable treatments remain an important area of training, but practitioner interest is also expanding into regenerative approaches, platelet-rich plasma (PRP), skin rejuvenation, ultrasound and other technology-assisted procedures.

These developments increase the importance of critical appraisal.

New treatments and products can attract significant attention before sufficient clinical evidence or consensus emerges to establish their appropriate use.

As a result, future training will need to cover more than procedural techniques. Practitioners will also need to learn how to assess evidence, select appropriate patients and recognise the limitations of emerging treatments.

Regional regulations remain important

Although clinical principles can be applied across borders, regulations vary between jurisdictions.

Scope of practice, licensing requirements and professional standards differ across GCC countries, meaning healthcare professionals remain responsible for understanding and complying with the rules governing their practice location.

Regional training centres can improve access to professional education, but not every healthcare professional can regularly travel to Dubai, Doha or another major city.

Online education therefore continues to have an important complementary role.

Foundational theory, treatment principles, anatomy, patient assessment frameworks and other knowledge-based components can be studied remotely, allowing practitioners to build their expertise regardless of location.

Healthcare professionals seeking flexible remote education can also explore online aesthetic medicine courses offered through CBAM’s international education platform and other medical education providers.

The key consideration is therefore not simply whether training takes place online or in person, but whether the educational format is appropriate for the competency being taught.

Training evolves with the sector

As aesthetic medicine across the Gulf becomes more sophisticated, professional education is also evolving.

Training programmes are placing greater emphasis on anatomy, clinical reasoning, evidence appraisal, patient selection, complication prevention and supervised practical experience alongside procedural techniques.

Dubai, Doha, Riyadh, and other Gulf cities may develop at different speeds, but practitioners, technologies and ideas increasingly connect these markets.

This is creating new opportunities for healthcare professionals to access specialised aesthetic medicine education within the region.
