title.rendered: HPPI presents model for dual TB-HIV integration at AIDS 2026 Conference

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

BY Shobha Shukla – CNS (Citizen News Service)

INDIA—Tuberculosis (TB) remains the most common opportunistic infection and a leading cause of death among people living with HIV, despite decades of progress in diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

Although TB is both preventable and curable, more than 150,000 people living with HIV died from TB in 2024, according to the latest UNAIDS report, launched at the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026).

“If we could have prevented TB better among people with HIV or found TB earlier and treated it with medicines that work against their TB bacteria, we could have saved these lives. No one needs to die of TB or HIV,” said the Prevent-Find-Treat ALL TB campaign.

More than 570,000 people died from AIDS-related illnesses in 2025.

The challenge extends beyond the availability of effective medical tools. Health systems must also identify people early and connect them with appropriate care before disease progresses, while protecting their dignity and right to health.

Experiences shared by experts from Humana People to People India (HPPI) at AIDS 2026 suggest that India could address this gap by integrating the latest science and evidence-based TB services into established HIV care and prevention platforms. The approach focuses on person-centred care and community leadership rather than creating entirely new programmes.

HPPI National Partnership Officer Jahangeer Alam, a TB survivor and TB champion, and National Technical Advisor for TB, HIV and Health Dr Sugata Mukhopadhyay described how stronger collaboration between the Government of India’s National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) and National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) is helping to identify TB earlier, improve treatment completion and put people, rather than diseases, at the centre of healthcare.

Why TB can be difficult to detect in People Living with HIV

According to Alam, TB remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV and accounts for about one in four HIV-related deaths globally.

However, TB in people living with HIV does not always present with the symptoms traditionally associated with the disease. Some people may not experience persistent cough, fever, weight loss or other commonly recognised symptoms.

As a result, health systems that rely primarily on symptom-based screening can miss infections until the disease has progressed.

Delayed diagnosis can worsen health outcomes and increase the risk of continued transmission. At the same time, TB screening is not always fully integrated into routine HIV care and antiretroviral therapy (ART) services.

Persistent stigma associated with both HIV and TB can further discourage people from seeking care early. Consequently, integrating the two services is not simply a matter of improving efficiency; it is also a clinical and human rights priority.

Using existing HIV platforms to find TB earlier

To address these challenges, HPPI worked with government-run ART centres in Delhi and the NTEP to strengthen TB-HIV integration.

Rather than creating new systems, the organisation used existing HIV care platforms to actively screen people attending ART centres for TB.

Since December 7, 2024, the government’s TB programme has also incorporated a science- and evidence-based approach to case finding by deploying artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled handheld, ultraportable X-ray systems and offering upfront molecular testing to people with presumptive TB.

The programme has taken these technologies in mobile vans to high-risk communities across the country. According to the programme, this approach identified more than one million asymptomatic people with TB disease within a year, enabling them to receive diagnoses earlier than would have been possible through symptom-based approaches alone.

Between May and July 2026, HPPI screened 1,363 people living with HIV using a comprehensive 10-symptom verbal screening tool alongside chest X-ray assessments. People identified as having presumptive TB subsequently underwent upfront rapid molecular testing.

The screening identified 259 people with presumptive TB, all of whom received diagnostic testing. Twenty-one people were diagnosed with TB and promptly linked to treatment.

Notably, 12 of the 21 people diagnosed with TB, or 57%, had no symptoms.

For Alam, the finding highlighted why the absence of symptoms cannot be taken as evidence that TB is absent.

Without systematic screening that combines symptom assessment, chest X-ray and rapid molecular testing, more than half of these TB cases could potentially have remained undetected.

The experience also demonstrated that every interaction between people living with HIV and healthcare providers can provide an opportunity to identify TB before the disease becomes severe.

Extending TB services into HIV prevention networks

ART centres provide an important point of contact, but Mukhopadhyay highlighted another opportunity: India’s extensive community-based HIV prevention network.

The country’s HIV prevention programme currently reaches approximately 15.8 million people through Targeted Intervention projects, Link Worker Scheme projects, Opioid Substitution Therapy centres and other outreach platforms.

These populations include female sex workers, gay men and other men who have sex with men, transgender people, people who inject drugs, migrant workers and truckers. Many face an increased risk of HIV as well as vulnerabilities associated with TB.

Rather than establishing separate TB programmes for these groups, HPPI trained existing outreach workers to incorporate TB services into their routine activities.

Community workers received training to screen for TB symptoms, educate communities about TB and HIV, address stigma and establish referral pathways with the NTEP for diagnosis, treatment and preventive therapy.

The approach builds on relationships that already exist within communities. Instead of introducing unfamiliar healthcare workers, the programme uses outreach teams that understand where vulnerable populations live and work and where they seek support.

This familiarity can help build trust and encourage people to seek care.

Supporting patients beyond diagnosis

HPPI’s approach extends beyond identifying TB cases. Mukhopadhyay said the organisation supports people throughout the continuum of care, from diagnosis and treatment initiation to adherence and completion.

Where appropriate, the programme also supports TB preventive treatment for eligible household contacts and people living with HIV. Regular community-based follow-up helps underserved people navigate the journey from diagnosis to treatment and, ultimately, cure.

HPPI drew on experience from four projects: three Targeted Intervention projects in Delhi, Unnao in Uttar Pradesh and Kathakota in Telangana, as well as a Link Worker Scheme project in Lucknow.

Across these projects, the organisation integrated TB activities into routine HIV outreach without establishing a separate service-delivery structure.

Data from the five-year period between 2020 and 2025 showed the potential of the approach.

Among populations at high risk of HIV, more than 113,000 people were screened for TB symptoms. The screening resulted in 671 TB diagnoses, with all diagnosed individuals initiated on treatment and completing it successfully.

The programme also supported 433 eligible household contacts to complete TB preventive treatment, helping reduce their risk of developing active TB.

Among people living with HIV, more than 500 individuals were screened, 11 were diagnosed with TB and all were started on treatment. In addition, 301 eligible people living with HIV completed TB preventive treatment.

For Mukhopadhyay, however, the figures represent only part of the programme’s impact. He emphasised that the experience demonstrated how comprehensive TB services can be delivered through existing HIV programmes without establishing parallel systems or requiring substantial additional resources.

Strengthening the role of community health workers

Alam and Mukhopadhyay stressed that integration does not simply mean combining two health programmes. Instead, it involves making better use of existing systems, personnel and community networks.

HPPI strengthened the skills of frontline workers, expanded their responsibilities and improved coordination with government health programmes.

Community outreach workers became an important part of the model. Their responsibilities included screening for TB symptoms, providing health education, reducing stigma, facilitating referrals, following up on treatment, supporting adherence and assisting with contact investigations.

They also provided regular support to people and families who might otherwise struggle to navigate the healthcare system.

Because these workers already have trusted relationships within their communities, they can reach people who may avoid health facilities because of discrimination, fear or other social barriers.

This use of existing relationships also makes service integration more practical and potentially more cost-effective.

As Mukhopadhyay put it, the approach was about “doing things differently—not necessarily doing more things separately.”

Five actions for stronger TB-HIV integration

Alam and Mukhopadhyay identified five actions they believe can strengthen TB-HIV integration.

First, symptom-based screening alone is insufficient for people living with HIV. Additional diagnostic approaches, including chest X-rays and upfront rapid molecular testing, can identify TB in people who do not have obvious symptoms. All services should also remain person-centred, community-based, community-led and rights-based, while ensuring equitable access.

Second, every interaction with HIV services should provide an opportunity to screen for TB. Waiting until symptoms become severe can result in delayed diagnosis, higher healthcare costs, continued transmission and poorer outcomes.

Third, government HIV services and the NTEP need strong coordination. Screening has limited value if people do not receive rapid testing, timely treatment and support throughout their care.

Fourth, community-based outreach should remain a core component of TB and HIV programmes. Trusted frontline workers can help address stigma, improve awareness and maintain continuity of care beyond health facilities.

Finally, integration can make financial as well as public health sense. Existing health systems, trained personnel and established community platforms already provide much of the infrastructure required. Better coordination can therefore deliver greater impact without necessarily requiring substantially higher expenditure.

Moving from Disease-Centred to Person-Centred Care

Healthcare systems often organise services around individual diseases, but people experience health differently.

A person living with HIV does not experience TB, HIV, nutrition, mental health and other health concerns as separate programmes. Instead, these issues can intersect and affect the same person’s life.

Alam and Mukhopadhyay therefore argued that health services should reflect this reality.

When TB and HIV services operate independently, opportunities for early diagnosis, prevention and treatment can be missed. By integrating services, healthcare providers can identify problems earlier, provide more comprehensive care and coordinate interventions instead of operating in isolation.

The approach places greater emphasis on supporting people rather than managing diseases separately.

Building on existing health systems

As India continues its efforts to eliminate TB and AIDS by 2030, HPPI’s experience highlights an approach that builds on existing health infrastructure, HIV programmes and community networks.

The organisation’s projects show that integrating community-based TB screening, diagnosis, treatment and prevention into established HIV platforms can help identify otherwise undetected cases, support treatment completion and expand access to preventive care among vulnerable populations.

The experience also demonstrates the role that collaboration among national health programmes, community organisations and frontline workers can play in strengthening the continuum of care.

At AIDS 2026, Alam and Mukhopadhyay emphasised the importance of organising healthcare around people’s needs rather than around separate disease programmes.

In their view, coordinated TB and HIV services can help ensure earlier diagnosis, timely treatment, preventive care, and continued support for people living with HIV.

title.rendered: Mercy Ships’ Global Mercy begins 10-month surgical mission in Ghana

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

GHANA—The Global Mercy, the world’s largest purpose-built civilian hospital ship, has arrived at the Port of Tema to begin a 10-month field service in partnership with the Government of Ghana.

The arrival follows the vessel’s recent field service in Sierra Leone and scheduled annual maintenance.

During the mission, Mercy Ships will provide free specialised surgical care aboard the Global Mercy while working with Ghanaian health professionals to strengthen the country’s surgical capacity.

Welcoming Mercy Ships back to Ghana, President John Dramani Mahama said health is “the foundation of freedom” and the country’s “greatest public good.”

Although Ghana has one of West Africa’s stronger healthcare systems, millions of people still face barriers to timely, safe and affordable surgical care.

The country launched its National Surgical, Obstetric and Anaesthesia Plan (NSOAP) in 2024 to expand access to essential surgical services.

However, shortages and uneven distribution of specialists, together with capacity constraints at district hospitals, continue to limit access.

Free specialised surgery

Ghana’s Minister of Health, Hon. Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, said the NSOAP supports the government’s wider health-sector goals by integrating surgical, obstetric and anaesthesia services into the country’s universal health coverage strategy.

The plan also aims to help reduce maternal and child mortality, improve trauma management and strengthen emergency and critical care services.

The current mission marks Mercy Ships’ fifth field service in Ghana.

In addition to free surgery, the programme will provide training, mentoring and professional development for local healthcare workers.

Patients from across Ghana can apply for specialised procedures, including cleft lip and palate repair, tumour removal, cataract surgery, reconstructive plastic surgery, obstetric fistula repair, paediatric orthopaedic procedures and general surgery.

“Returning to Ghana is the continuation of a trusted partnership,” said Michael Nkeze, Mercy Ships Country Director for Ghana.

“Together with the Ministry of Health and our national partners, we are investing not only in life-changing surgery for today’s patients, but also in stronger surgical systems that will benefit future generations.”

Longstanding partnership

Mercy Ships first arrived in Ghana in 1991 and has since worked with the government to provide more than 2,670 surgical procedures and over 18,120 dental procedures.

The organisation has also trained more than 2,920 healthcare professionals and reached nearly 15,000 direct medical beneficiaries.

Volunteers from more than 70 countries staff the Global Mercy, bringing together surgeons, nurses, anaesthetists, engineers, teachers, cooks and maritime professionals.

Ghanaian volunteers remain an important part of the organisation.

Among them is Hospital Chaplain Clementine, known as “Mama,” who first encountered Mercy Ships in the 1990s and joined the crew in 1997.

With Ghanaian and Togolese roots, Clementine said the international volunteers she met inspired her to dedicate her life to serving African communities.

“Nearly 30 years ago, Mercy Ships captured my heart,” she said.

“Today, returning to Ghana feels like coming home. It is a privilege to serve my own people and to welcome every patient with dignity, compassion and hope.”

Over the next 10 months, international volunteers and Ghanaian healthcare professionals will work together to provide surgical care and strengthen Ghana’s healthcare workforce and surgical systems.

title.rendered: Kenya to build 10 specialized maternal and newborn facilities across high-burden counties

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Kenya is set to establish 10 specialised maternal and newborn health facilities in counties with the highest burden of preventable deaths as the government steps up efforts to improve access to quality care.

The 250-bed facilities will be built in Nairobi, Bomet, Kwale, Mombasa, Garissa, Kisumu, Embu, Nakuru, West Pokot and Uasin Gishu.

The centres will provide comprehensive services, including antenatal and postnatal care, labour and recovery services, obstetric care, Caesarean sections, theatres, maternal and neonatal intensive care, neonatal intensive care units and post-Caesarean wards.

The facilities will be designed to link routine maternity services with emergency and specialised care under one system.

This integrated model will enable mothers and newborns needing additional support to receive timely referrals and treatment without unnecessary delays, while county health teams coordinate services with national authorities throughout implementation.

The initiative follows bilateral discussions between Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale and county leaders, led by Council of Governors Health Committee Chairperson and Mombasa Governor Abdullswamad Nassir.

The talks focused on implementing President William Ruto’s directive to prioritise maternal and newborn health.

Funding and targeted investment

Amsons Group will provide KES 4.4 billion (US$34.0 million) through the Mama na Mtoto Kwanza initiative, in partnership with the government.

The investment complements the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere programme and will expand access to specialised maternal and newborn services.

The government selected the locations after mapping 26 counties that account for about 60% of Kenya’s maternal deaths.

The targeted approach is intended to direct infrastructure and specialised services to areas with the greatest need while supporting Kenya’s Universal Health Coverage agenda.

In addition, KES 4 billion (US$30.9 million) is being channelled through the Social Health Authority to support maternal deliveries at Level 2 and Level 3 facilities.

The funding is expected to widen access to safe maternity services closer to communities.

Expanding the healthcare workforce

The infrastructure programme is being accompanied by efforts to increase the number of skilled health workers available to provide maternal and newborn care.

Under the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere programme, 900 healthcare workers have already received training in obstetric care, while another 900 have been trained in comprehensive newborn care.

The Government is also recruiting 5,000 nurses and midwives to strengthen staffing levels and support the expanded maternity and neonatal services.

County coordination and implementation

Groundbreaking for the new facilities is expected by September, with the national and county governments working to coordinate implementation.

Discussions also focused on accelerating project delivery and ensuring the planned facilities respond to local healthcare needs.

The meeting brought together Kisumu Governor Anyang’ Nyong’o and Embu Governor Cecily Mbarire; Bomet Deputy Governor Shadrack Rotich and West Pokot Deputy Governor Achaule Robert; and county officials, including Kisumu County Executive Committee Member Dr Gregory Ganda.

Ministry of Health officials attending the meeting included Director for Family Health Dr Bashir Issak, Presidential Advisor on Health Wilson Aruasa and Head of Infrastructure, Projects and Grants Management Dr Hezron Omolo, alongside other ministry representatives.

title.rendered: Yas Clinic partners with ADSCC to expand access to complex pediatric bone marrow transplants in UAE

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—Doctors at Yas Clinic, in collaboration with the Abu Dhabi Stem Cells Center (ADSCC), have successfully treated a 13-month-old child with a rare inherited immune disorder through an urgent bone marrow transplant using stem cells donated by his father.

The procedure marks another milestone for the UAE in treating complex pediatric immune disorders and expanding access to advanced bone marrow transplantation.

The child began experiencing recurrent, severe infections during the first months of life, resulting in several prolonged hospital admissions.

He also struggled to gain weight and developed a severe skin condition that caused widespread redness and continuous peeling, making his skin resemble that of a patient with extensive burns.

Further investigations identified a rare inherited immunodeficiency caused by a homozygous mutation in the RAG1 gene, which was associated with Omenn syndrome.

The condition severely disrupts immune function and leaves affected children highly vulnerable to potentially life-threatening infections.

The family’s medical history, which included the death of a sibling from a similar condition, prompted an accelerated diagnostic and treatment process.

The child was subsequently referred to the Abu Dhabi Bone Marrow Transplant Program (AD-BMT©) for urgent care.

Father serves as stem-cell donor

Comprehensive donor testing found that the child had no fully matched sibling donor. Tissue-typing studies showed that both parents were half-matched donors.

Because of the child’s critical condition and the continuing risk from severe infections, the multidisciplinary team opted for a haploidentical bone marrow transplant using stem cells donated by his father.

The procedure resulted in successful engraftment and a gradual restoration of the child’s immune function.

His clinical condition improved significantly, with his severe skin symptoms resolving and recurrent infections subsiding. He was subsequently discharged from hospital and continued to recover, gain weight and improve his overall health.

Dr. Maysoon Al Karam, Chief Medical Officer at Yas Clinic, said the case demonstrates the impact of combining specialized medical expertise with advanced treatment capabilities.

“Successfully treating a child with such a rare and complex immunological condition demonstrates our continued commitment to delivering the highest standards of care and further reinforces Abu Dhabi’s position as a regional center of excellence in medical innovation and advanced healthcare,” she said.

She added that the case highlights the capabilities of the Abu Dhabi Bone Marrow Transplant Program in managing complex conditions through multidisciplinary expertise and treatment protocols aligned with international best practices.

Early diagnosis proves critical

Dr. Mansi Sachdev, Consultant Pediatric Hematology, Oncology and Bone Marrow Transplantation at ADSCC, said the child arrived at the center with severe immunodeficiency that left him vulnerable to life-threatening infections.

“Given the nature of the disease and the family’s medical history, urgent intervention was critical. Through accurate diagnosis, close multidisciplinary collaboration and a bone marrow transplant from his father, we were able to rebuild his immune system and give him an opportunity to grow and live a healthy life,” she said.

Sachdev emphasized the importance of early diagnosis and specialized treatment for children with rare inherited immune disorders.

She added that the program continues to provide advanced treatment options for children with complex conditions in the UAE.

Yas Clinic and ADSCC provide treatment for blood disorders, immune deficiencies and rare genetic diseases through the Abu Dhabi Bone Marrow Transplant Program, which offers bone marrow transplantation and advanced cellular therapies.

title.rendered: M.P. Shah Hospital names Dr. Kalpesh Patel as new board chairman

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—M.P. Shah Hospital has appointed Dr. Kalpesh Patel as its new Chairman of the Board of Directors, with Mr. Mahesh Chandaria serving as co-chair.

The leadership changes are part of the hospital’s ongoing efforts to strengthen governance and support the implementation of its strategic vision.

The appointments will see Dr. Patel take over the chairmanship from Dr. Manoj Shah, who has led the Board through a period of significant development for the Nairobi-based hospital.

Mr. Chandaria will serve alongside Dr. Patel as Co-Chair, providing additional leadership and oversight as the institution continues to expand its healthcare services and strengthen its position in Kenya’s private healthcare sector.

Leadership Transition

The hospital said the new leadership structure reflects the Board’s commitment to strong, values-driven governance and continuity as M.P. Shah Hospital pursues its long-term objectives.

The institution also expressed its appreciation to Dr. Manoj Shah for his leadership, guidance and commitment during his tenure as Chairman.

Under his leadership, the hospital recorded several milestones in clinical excellence, patient-centred care and sustainability.

One of the key achievements during his tenure was the hospital’s recognition as a Joint Commission International (JCI)-accredited institution.

JCI accreditation recognises healthcare organisations that meet internationally recognised standards for quality and patient safety.

Following the leadership transition, Dr. Manoj Shah will remain actively involved with the hospital. He will serve as an Honorary Board Member and Immediate Past Chairman, while also retaining his position on the Executive Committee.

New Chapter for M.P. Shah Hospital

Commenting on the changes, Dr. Toseef Din, Chief Executive Officer of M.P. Shah Hospital, welcomed the incoming leaders and acknowledged Dr. Manoj Shah’s contribution to the institution.

“We warmly welcome Dr. Patel and Mr. Chandaria, and we thank Dr. Shah for his outstanding service and leadership,” said Dr. Din.

The CEO said the leadership transition would build on the hospital’s existing foundation while supporting its continued development and impact.

Dr. Patel’s appointment comes as M.P. Shah Hospital continues to focus on delivering high-quality healthcare while strengthening its organisational systems and services.

The Board will work with hospital management to advance the institution’s strategic priorities and maintain its focus on patient-centred care.

The hospital said the new leadership team would continue to support its commitment to clinical excellence, responsible governance and sustainable growth.

At the same time, Dr. Manoj Shah’s continued involvement through his roles on the Board and Executive Committee will provide institutional continuity during the transition.

M.P. Shah Hospital has served patients in Kenya for decades and provides a range of medical and specialist healthcare services.

The institution’s latest leadership changes mark a shift in Board responsibilities while retaining experienced leadership within its governance structure.

With Dr. Patel assuming the chairmanship and Mr. Chandaria taking on the role of co-chair, the hospital will continue implementing its strategic priorities under the oversight of the Board of Directors.

title.rendered: ECOWAS hands over new maternity and pediatric complex in Guinea-Bissau

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

GUINEA-BISSAU—The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) has handed over a new Maternity and Paediatric Complex at Bafatá Regional Hospital, strengthening access to maternal and child healthcare in one of Guinea-Bissau’s regions where such services remain limited.

The technical handover and symbolic presentation of the facility’s keys took place on 8 August 2026.

ECOWAS financed the project through its Regional Fund for Stabilisation and Development (FRSD), investing US$638,538.05 in the new facility.

New capacity for mothers and children

The complex includes dedicated maternity and paediatric areas, with a total capacity of 66 beds and several functional units designed to improve patient reception, treatment, and care.

ECOWAS Vice President Damtien Larbli Tchintchibidja said the investment reflects the organization’s commitment to ensuring safer childbirth, healthier childhoods, and stronger communities across the region.

The project involved Kozan Limited Company and Baga-Baga Construções SARL, which carried out the construction works as a consortium. Competent authorities in Guinea-Bissau and the ECOWAS FRSD team supervised the works.

At the ceremony, Guinea-Bissau’s Minister of Economy, Planning and Regional Integration Mamadu Mudjetaba Djalo, Bafatá Governor Mustafa Soares Cassam and other senior government officials welcomed the facility and commended ECOWAS for supporting healthcare infrastructure in the region.

Facility begins phased commissioning

Following the handover ceremony, officials and project partners attended a presentation on the construction of the complex before touring the new maternity and paediatric units.

The new facility is expected to improve conditions for pregnant women, mothers, newborns, and children by providing dedicated spaces for consultations, treatment and follow-up.

It will also expand Bafatá Regional Hospital’s capacity to respond to the healthcare needs of communities in the region and surrounding areas.

Part of wider regional development programme

The Bafatá complex forms part of the broader FRSD programme, which ECOWAS established with support from the German Government through the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ).

The fund supports projects designed to create sustainable economic and social opportunities while strengthening the resilience of communities in fragile regions of ECOWAS member states.

Following the handover, the ECOWAS delegation visited other projects in Bafatá implemented under the organisation’s QUICK IMPACT initiative.

These included an automatic brickmaking facility financed for a youth association to support employment and an automatic rice-winnowing facility for a women’s farming group.

Through these projects, ECOWAS is supporting healthcare, employment and agricultural activities while strengthening essential services and economic opportunities for communities across the region.

title.rendered: Mayo Clinic study uncovers mechanism behind resistance to HER2 breast cancer drug

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”124px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”-102px|||||” custom_padding=”0px|||||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE— Mayo Clinic researchers have identified a mechanism that may explain why some HER2-positive (HER2+) breast cancers fail to respond to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that has improved outcomes for many patients with advanced disease.

The study, published in Nature Cancer, found that a shortened form of the HER2 protein, known as p95HER2, can alter how cancer cells respond to T-DXd.

The researchers say the finding could help guide the development of more targeted treatment combinations for patients whose tumors produce the protein.

Shortened HER2 protein linked to resistance

ADCs combine a cancer-targeting antibody with a potent chemotherapy drug to deliver treatment directly to tumor cells.

However, although T-DXd has demonstrated significant benefits in HER2+ breast cancer, some patients eventually fail to respond to the treatment.

Researchers in Mayo Clinic’s Oncoimmune Signaling and Therapeutics Laboratory investigated the biological mechanisms that could contribute to this resistance.

They found that p95HER2, which occurs in a subset of HER2+ breast cancers, behaves differently from the full-length HER2 protein.

According to the researchers, p95HER2 triggers distinct cellular signals that can create an immune-protected environment around cancer cells.

This signaling may allow tumor cells to withstand the effects of T-DXd.

“While T-DXd has shown remarkable results for many patients, it hasn’t worked for everyone with advanced HER2+ breast cancer,” said Peter Lucas, M.D., Ph.D., vice chair for research in the Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology at Mayo Clinic and co-senior author of the study.

The findings suggest that p95HER2 does more than simply indicate the presence of HER2 in a tumor.

Instead, the protein may actively contribute to treatment resistance by changing the tumor’s biological environment.

Neratinib targets p95HER2

The researchers also examined whether existing medicines could interfere with p95HER2 activity. Their experiments identified neratinib as a potentially effective option.

In preclinical models, neratinib blocked p95HER2 signaling and led to complete degradation of the shortened protein in cancer cells.

“Treatment with neratinib results in complete p95HER2 degradation, abolishing the protein from the cancer cells in our preclinical models,” said Dong Hu, Ph.D., a research scientist in Laboratory Medicine and Pathology at Mayo Clinic and lead author.

Based on the findings, the researchers are considering a clinical trial combining neratinib with T-DXd in patients with HER2+ early breast cancer.

The proposed study would assess whether the combination can improve treatment responses in tumors that produce both p95HER2 and the full-length HER2 protein.

The research team emphasized that this combination represents one of several potential treatment strategies for HER2+ breast cancer.

“No single, one-size-fits-all approach to treatment will work for every patient with HER2+ breast cancer,” said Linda McAllister, M.D., Ph.D., a pediatric hematologist/oncologist at Mayo Clinic and co-senior author.

The researchers said understanding how p95HER2 influences treatment response could support the development of customized therapeutic approaches for patients whose tumors express the shortened protein.

title.rendered: New King Nyabela Hospital opens in Mpumalanga to serve 240,000 residents

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”124px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”-102px|||||” custom_padding=”0px|||||” global_colors_info=”{}”]

SOUTH AFRICA—President Cyril Ramaphosa, accompanied by Minister of Health Aaron Motsoaledi, has officially inaugurated the new King Nyabela Hospital in Mpumalanga, marking a significant milestone in South Africa’s efforts to strengthen public healthcare services.

Named after King Nyabela of the Ndzundza-Ndebele people, the 220-bed district hospital will provide essential healthcare services to more than 240,000 residents of the Steve Tshwete Local Municipality.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Ramaphosa described healthcare as a fundamental human right that enables every citizen to live with dignity.

He noted that South Africa’s Constitution guarantees everyone access to healthcare services and requires the state to take reasonable measures, within available resources, to progressively realize this right.

According to the president, the completion of King Nyabela Hospital demonstrates the government’s commitment to expanding access to quality healthcare across the country.

Comprehensive healthcare services

The newly commissioned hospital offers a broad range of inpatient and outpatient services designed to meet the healthcare needs of the surrounding communities.

Its inpatient facilities include surgical, medical, paediatric, antenatal, postnatal, neonatal and high-care wards, supported by three operating theatres and a modern accident and emergency department.

Outpatient services include a pharmacy, tuberculosis (TB) and HIV management, dentistry, eye care, dietetics and nutrition, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, social work, mental health services and medical male circumcision, among other essential healthcare programs.

Ramaphosa said the extensive range of services reflects the government’s vision of comprehensive healthcare, which extends beyond treating illness.

He explained that quality healthcare also focuses on disease prevention, early diagnosis, long-term management of medical conditions and promoting healthy lives from childhood through old age.

He added that comprehensive care addresses both physical and mental well-being while supporting patients throughout every stage of life.

Strengthening National Health Insurance

The president also reaffirmed the government’s commitment to implementing the National Health Insurance (NHI), describing it as a key step toward achieving universal health coverage.

He said the NHI aims to ensure that access to healthcare no longer depends on where people live or their financial circumstances.

Under the NHI framework, the government will establish a centralized national insurance fund that will purchase healthcare services from both public and private healthcare providers.

Ramaphosa said the system is intended to give all South Africans access to the full range of quality healthcare services they need without facing financial hardship.

He emphasized that the success of the NHI will depend on effective governance, strong leadership, a skilled healthcare workforce, consistently high standards of service delivery and uninterrupted access to medicines.

Commitment to accountability and quality care

Ramaphosa stressed that all hospitals and clinics commissioned under the NHI programme must be completed on schedule and within approved budgets. He noted that King Nyabela Hospital met both targets, demonstrating that major public health infrastructure projects can be delivered efficiently.

The president also reiterated the government’s determination to eliminate corruption, fraud and waste in the procurement of healthcare infrastructure, medical supplies and services.

While acknowledging progress in recovering stolen funds and prosecuting suspected offenders, he said authorities remain committed to strengthening accountability across the health sector.

Ramaphosa concluded by recognizing the dedication of healthcare professionals, noting that although hospitals are built with bricks and mortar, their true strength comes from the doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers who continue serving patients despite challenging conditions.

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.7″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”124px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”-102px|||||” custom_padding=”0px|||||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

USA—Exer AI, a company that uses computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse human movement, is expanding its partnership with Mayo Clinic to deploy its technology in orthopaedic workflows across the academic healthcare system.

The Colorado-based company’s Exer Scan App uses cameras on smartphones, tablets and laptops to capture joint movement and mobility data.

Through the expanded partnership, Mayo Clinic will clinically integrate Exer AI’s hand and wrist module into its orthopaedic workflows to support musculoskeletal care.

AI-powered movement assessment

The hand and wrist module can be used during in-person and virtual visits to assess mobility, strength proxies and range of motion through a camera-based examination.

The technology is designed to fit into clinicians’ existing workflows and automatically transfer assessment results into patients’ electronic health records through Epic.

Exer Scan is natively integrated with Epic’s electronic health record system and can send assessment results directly to an Epic SmartNote to support clinical documentation.

The platform also connects with Epic’s billing system to facilitate coding and reimbursement.

According to Zaw Thet, CEO and cofounder of Exer AI, the company began developing its computer vision technology in 2018.

Its researchers trained a neural network to recognize the human body using cameras placed in gyms, physical therapy clinics and doctors’ offices.

The company collected millions of hours of video footage and analyzed it frame by frame, manually identifying body parts to train the AI model.

Exer AI subsequently used the technology to determine how specific movement patterns could indicate different medical conditions.

Expanding clinical applications

To develop these capabilities, Exer AI established research partnerships covering 14 medical disciplines, including orthopedics, neurosurgery, pain management and spine care.

The company has since developed about 144 assessments covering movements and functions such as tremors, sit-to-stand performance, balance, joint range of motion, gait dynamics and functional movement.

Mayo Clinic became one of Exer AI’s early research partners when the organizations began collaborating in 2024.

The latest agreement moves the relationship further into clinical deployment by incorporating the company’s hand and wrist assessment technology into orthopedic care.

Thet said the partnership could also provide a pathway for Exer AI to expand its technology across a network of about 40 other hospital and healthcare systems associated with the Mayo Clinic platform.

New modules in development

Exer AI plans to broaden its technology to additional clinical applications.

The company is developing a sports medicine module focused on athletes returning to sport, which Thet expects to launch by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

The company also plans to continue developing additional assessments and expanding the range of conditions that its AI-powered movement analysis can evaluate.

title.rendered: Ministry of Defense performs Saudi Arabia’s first Riyadh-Dhahran remote robotic surgery

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”132px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”-102px|||||” custom_padding=”0px|||||” global_colors_info=”{}”]

SAUDI ARABIA—The Health Services of the Ministry of Defense has conducted Saudi Arabia’s first remote robotic surgery between two of its healthcare facilities in Riyadh and Dhahran, with technical support from stc group.

The procedure used advanced digital infrastructure and high-reliability communications technology to connect medical teams at the two facilities, enabling specialists to perform surgery remotely despite the geographical distance between the sites.

The operation demonstrated how digital connectivity can support the delivery of specialist surgical care across regions.

It also brought together medical teams and technical specialists responsible for networks and digital infrastructure to ensure that the procedure was carried out safely and accurately.

Secure digital infrastructure

stc group designed and operated the integrated digital communications system supporting the procedure.

The system provided a secure, high-reliability network connecting the operating rooms at both healthcare facilities and integrating the technical systems required for the surgery.

The network enabled the real-time transmission of medical data and imaging while supporting remote control of the robotic surgical system.

According to stc group, the infrastructure allowed these processes to take place with high levels of efficiency and precision.

The successful procedure highlights the role of reliable digital connectivity in enabling remote access to specialist medical expertise.

By linking healthcare facilities over secure communications networks, remote robotic surgery could help specialists provide advanced surgical services to patients who may otherwise need to travel to another city for treatment.

Supporting healthcare transformation

The collaboration between the Ministry of Defense Health Services and stc group forms part of Saudi Arabia’s wider efforts to use digital technologies to develop its healthcare system.

The initiative supports the expansion of specialist healthcare services across the country while strengthening the technological infrastructure underpinning healthcare delivery.

The remote procedure also demonstrates the potential for closer integration between healthcare providers and technology companies as digital tools become increasingly important in clinical settings.

In this case, the combination of medical expertise, robotic surgery and high-speed communications infrastructure enabled a surgical team to operate across geographically separated facilities.

The achievement aligns with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, which seeks to improve the accessibility and quality of healthcare services while accelerating digital transformation across the health sector.

title.rendered: AGC Tenwek Hospital performs Kenya’s first keyhole surgery on newborn

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA— AGC Tenwek Hospital has successfully performed what it says is Kenya’s first keyhole surgery on a newborn, marking a significant milestone in the country’s pediatric surgical care.

The procedure was led by Dr. Daniel Tamirat Cherkos, a consultant pediatric surgeon at the hospital, who worked with a multidisciplinary surgical team to perform the minimally invasive operation on the newborn.

Milestone in pediatric surgery

Keyhole surgery, also known as minimally invasive surgery, involves making small incisions through which surgeons insert specialized instruments and a camera to perform an operation.

Compared with conventional open surgery, the technique can reduce surgical trauma and may support faster recovery.

Performing such a procedure on a newborn requires highly specialized surgical expertise because of the patient’s small size and the technical challenges associated with operating on delicate tissues and organs.

Tenwek Hospital congratulated Dr. Cherkos and the surgical team for successfully completing the procedure and described the achievement as an important advancement in pediatric surgical care in Kenya.

The hospital said the milestone reflects the team’s dedication to improving treatment options for some of the country’s youngest and most vulnerable patients.

Advancing specialized care

According to the hospital, the achievement resulted from extensive preparation, technical expertise and a commitment to introducing innovative approaches to surgical care.

Dr. Cherkos and his colleagues have worked to expand access to specialized pediatric surgical services, with the latest procedure demonstrating the potential for advanced minimally invasive techniques to be used in newborn care.

The hospital praised the team for combining surgical skill with careful planning and a commitment to patient safety.

“Behind this milestone is not just surgical skill, but countless hours of dedication, courage, innovation and an unwavering commitment to the smallest and most vulnerable patients entrusted to your care,” the hospital said.

The successful operation also highlights the growing capacity of Kenyan healthcare institutions to undertake complex procedures that require highly specialized expertise and advanced surgical techniques.

Recognition for the surgical team

Tenwek Hospital said Dr. Cherkos’ leadership played a central role in achieving the milestone, while also recognizing the contribution of the wider surgical team involved in the procedure.

The hospital described the achievement as the result of teamwork, professional dedication, and a willingness to push the boundaries of what is possible in pediatric medicine.

It also commended the team for providing care to a newborn who required specialized surgical intervention, emphasizing the importance of innovation in improving outcomes for children and their families.

“On behalf of the entire Tenwek Hospital family, we celebrate you, the incredible surgical team, and this historic achievement,” the hospital said.

The hospital further expressed its appreciation to Dr. Cherkos and the entire team for their contribution to advancing pediatric surgical care in Kenya.

The procedure adds to the range of specialized services available at AGC Tenwek Hospital and underscores the institution’s focus on developing advanced surgical capabilities for patients requiring complex care.

title.rendered: Medcare Dubai launches patient-specific 3D-printed surgical guides for spine care

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE— Medcare Orthopaedics and Spine Hospital in Dubai has introduced patient-specific 3D-printed surgical guides for complex spinal procedures, marking a major advancement in spine care.

The technology is designed to improve surgical precision, shorten operating times, reduce blood loss, and accelerate recovery for patients with severe scoliosis and other spinal deformities.

The development further strengthens the UAE’s position as a regional hub for advanced spinal treatment.

Among the first patients to benefit from the new approach were two girls aged 14 and 15 and a 17-year-old boy, all diagnosed with severe scoliosis that required complex corrective surgery.

Personalised planning improves surgical outcomes

Dr. Sameh Abolfotouh, Consultant Orthopaedic and Spine Surgeon at Medcare Orthopaedics and Spine Hospital and Chairperson of AO Spine for the Middle East and Africa (MEA) region, said every scoliosis case presents unique challenges, making personalised surgical planning essential.

He explained that the 14-year-old patient had severe spinal curvature affecting both the upper and lower spine after experiencing persistent back pain.

Using detailed pre-operative planning and customised 3D-printed guides, the surgical team achieved precise correction, enabling her to return to normal daily activities.

The 17-year-old patient had a significant spinal deformity that threatened his posture and long-term mobility.

According to Dr. Abolfotouh, the technology enabled surgeons to complete the complex procedure in just four hours, compared with the traditional eight to ten hours often required for similar operations, without post-operative complications.

Meanwhile, the 15-year-old girl had a progressive spinal curvature exceeding 50 degrees.

The customised guides allowed surgeons to accurately navigate her spinal anatomy, restore alignment, and support a smooth recovery.

Digital workflow enhances precision

Dr. Abolfotouh said the customised 3D-printed guides reduce surgery duration by more than half while improving accuracy during corrective procedures. As a result, young patients can return more quickly to school, sports, work, and other daily activities with fewer complications.

Dr. Azzam Fayyad, Consultant Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgeon, Medical Director, and Head of Orthopaedics at Medcare Orthopaedics and Spine Hospital, explained that the hospital has implemented a specialised digital workflow that allows surgeons to virtually plan each operation before entering the operating theatre.

The process begins with advanced imaging to create detailed three-dimensional models of each patient’s spine. These images are then used to manufacture customised surgical guides that precisely match the patient’s anatomy.

During surgery, the guides fit onto the vertebrae like a lock and key, enabling surgeons to place implants with exceptional precision while reducing the margin of error to less than two per cent.

Faster recovery with less blood loss

According to Dr. Fayyad, the hospital uses the technology to minimise operating time, reduce blood loss, and support faster recovery for both paediatric and adult patients with complex spinal conditions.

He noted that one of the hospital’s primary focus areas is the treatment of Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS), a progressive condition that causes abnormal spinal curvature during childhood and adolescence.

In severe cases, AIS can affect posture, mobility, self-confidence, and overall quality of life, often making major corrective surgery necessary.

Traditionally, these procedures last between eight and ten hours and involve substantial blood loss, extended hospitalisation, and lengthy rehabilitation.

Dr. Abolfotouh added that the virtual planning process allows surgeons to simulate the entire procedure before entering the operating room, ensuring that every surgical step is carefully mapped in advance.

The technology has also significantly reduced blood loss to less than 400 millilitres per procedure, lowering the need for major blood transfusions and reducing the risk of complications.

These improvements contribute to safer operations and faster recovery for both children and adults undergoing complex spinal surgery.

title.rendered: Bupa CareConnect expands integrated digital healthcare network across Saudi Arabia

[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

SAUDI ARABIA—Bupa CareConnect is strengthening its role in Saudi Arabia’s rapidly evolving healthcare sector by expanding an integrated care model that combines digital technology, strategic partnerships and patient-centred services.

As the healthcare delivery arm of Bupa Arabia for Cooperative Insurance Company, the organization is broadening access to medical services while supporting better health outcomes through connected care.

Since its launch in 2024, Bupa CareConnect has developed a healthcare ecosystem that links medical consultations, virtual care, home laboratory testing, medication delivery and chronic disease management into a seamless patient journey.

The company reported that demand for its digital consultation services has increased more than fivefold over the past year, highlighting the growing adoption of virtual healthcare across the Kingdom.

Building a connected healthcare ecosystem

Bupa CareConnect has partnered with several healthcare providers to make medical services more convenient and accessible.

Through its collaboration with Al Borg Diagnostics, members can schedule laboratory tests at home, reducing the need to visit healthcare facilities while encouraging earlier diagnosis and routine health monitoring.

The company has also expanded its pharmacy network through partnerships with Nahdi Pharmacy and Al-Dawaa.

These collaborations allow prescribed medications to be delivered directly to patients, improving treatment adherence and ensuring continuity of care, particularly for individuals managing long-term conditions.

By integrating diagnostics, pharmacy services and virtual consultations into a single healthcare journey, Bupa CareConnect aims to simplify access to healthcare while enabling healthcare professionals to coordinate patient care more effectively.

Strengthening chronic disease management

Managing chronic diseases remains a key focus of the company’s healthcare strategy.

Its Chronic Care Management programmes, particularly those designed for people living with diabetes, have demonstrated measurable improvements in disease control and key health indicators.

The programmes combine early diagnosis, preventive care, primary healthcare services, virtual consultations and continuous medical follow-up to help patients better manage their conditions.

This coordinated approach enables healthcare providers to intervene earlier, monitor patient progress more closely and reduce the risk of complications while maintaining consistent standards of care.

Patients can also enrol in preventive health and disease management programmes through Bupa CareConnect’s digital platforms.

These online services simplify registration, facilitate ongoing communication between patients and healthcare providers, and support timely responses to changing healthcare needs.

Expanding digital healthcare services

A central component of the integrated care model is the Bupa Digital Clinic, which provides round-the-clock medical consultations.

Staffed by highly qualified Saudi physicians representing more than 12 medical specialties, the clinic allows members to receive professional medical advice without travelling to a healthcare facility.

The virtual platform improves access to healthcare regardless of a patient’s location while supporting faster clinical decision-making and more consistent follow-up care.

Bupa CareConnect is also advancing its digital primary healthcare strategy by incorporating artificial intelligence-powered healthcare solutions into its platform.

These technologies help personalise patient engagement, encourage adherence to prescribed treatment plans and support more efficient coordination between healthcare providers.

As Saudi Arabia continues to modernise its healthcare system under Vision 2030, Bupa CareConnect is expanding beyond the traditional role of a health insurer by delivering integrated healthcare services.

Its connected model brings together preventive care, diagnosis, treatment and follow-up through a digitally enabled network that links patients with healthcare providers throughout every stage of their healthcare journey.

KENYA— Nyamira County Referral Hospital (NCRH) has performed its first total hip replacement surgeries, marking a significant step in the county’s efforts to expand access to specialised orthopaedic care.

The hospital successfully conducted two total hip replacement procedures in a carefully planned three-hour operation led by a multidisciplinary team of specialists.

The surgeries involved patients who had been living with debilitating hip conditions that affected their mobility and quality of life.

Following the procedures, the patients will undergo a structured rehabilitation programme aimed at helping them regain mobility, manage their recovery and return to their daily activities.

Expanding access to specialised care

Nyamira County Governor Amos Nyaribo said the achievement demonstrates the growing capacity of the county’s health system to provide complex medical procedures locally.

He commended the team led by Dr Jared Oeba, an orthopaedic surgeon and County Director for Medical Services, as well as the surgical, anaesthesia, nursing and rehabilitation teams involved in the procedures.

The new service will reduce the need for patients requiring complex joint replacement procedures to travel to referral hospitals outside Nyamira County.

Previously, such patients often faced additional financial and emotional burdens associated with seeking specialised treatment far from home.

“With this milestone, Nyamira County Referral Hospital now has the capacity, expertise and infrastructure to routinely offer total hip replacement surgery,” Nyaribo said.

Total hip replacement involves removing damaged portions of the hip joint and replacing them with artificial components to restore joint function.

The procedure can help patients with severely damaged or worn-out hip joints resulting from conditions such as trauma, arthritis and other degenerative diseases.

More procedures planned

The county has already scheduled several additional patients for total hip replacement procedures, indicating plans to expand the availability of advanced orthopaedic services at the facility.

According to the governor, the development forms part of his administration’s broader investment in strengthening healthcare infrastructure, equipping medical facilities and expanding access to specialised services within the county.

The county government said building local capacity for complex procedures will allow residents to receive specialised treatment closer to home while reducing the need for referrals to distant facilities.

Nyaribo also commended the Department of Health Services, led by County Executive Committee Member for Health Services Dr Donald Mogoi, and the entire Nyamira County Referral Hospital team for delivering the procedures.

The introduction of total hip replacement surgery adds to the range of specialised services available at the county referral facility and reflects continued efforts to strengthen its surgical and rehabilitation capabilities.

title.rendered: Moderna begins Phase 1 trial of mRNA vaccine against Bundibugyo Ebola

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

USA—Moderna has begun vaccinating participants in a Phase 1 clinical trial of mRNA-1469, an investigational vaccine targeting Bundibugyo ebolavirus, a strain of Ebola for which no approved vaccine currently exists.

Health Canada authorized the study, which is being conducted at three sites across Canada and is expected to enroll about 80 healthy adults.

The trial will assess the vaccine’s safety, tolerability and ability to generate an immune response, according to Moderna.

mRNA vaccine enters clinical testing

The vaccine candidate uses Moderna’s mRNA technology platform, the same technology the company used to develop its COVID-19 vaccine.

The approach delivers genetic instructions that prompt cells to produce a target antigen, enabling the immune system to recognize and respond to the virus.

The Phase 1 study forms part of an expanded collaboration between Moderna and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI).

Under the agreement, CEPI has committed up to US$50 million to support preclinical development and the Phase 1 trial, while also supporting the manufacture of additional clinical doses in parallel with early-stage testing.

This strategy is designed to allow larger Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials to begin rapidly if the initial study produces results that support further development.

“Vaccinating the first participants with mRNA-1469 marks an important milestone in advancing a vaccine candidate against Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which no approved vaccine currently exists,” Moderna Chief Executive Officer Stéphane Bancel said.

Ebola outbreak drives vaccine development

The Bundibugyo strain is responsible for the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.

 As of August 1, the outbreak had resulted in 3,748 confirmed cases and 1,657 confirmed deaths, according to figures cited by Reuters from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The World Health Organization and Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention have declared the outbreak a public health emergency.

CEPI Chief Executive Officer Dr Richard Hatchett said cases are increasing faster than during the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola epidemic, which remains the largest Ebola outbreak recorded.

The outbreak has intensified efforts to develop vaccines against Bundibugyo ebolavirus because existing licensed Ebola vaccines target other strains, particularly Zaire ebolavirus.

Moderna’s candidate is among several vaccine programmes being advanced in response to the outbreak.

CEPI-backed vaccine programmes

Moderna and CEPI announced their expanded partnership earlier this year, with CEPI also supporting vaccine development by the University of Oxford and the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative.

The programmes use different vaccine technologies as developers seek to accelerate the availability of protection against the Bundibugyo strain.

Oxford’s vaccine candidate, ChAdOx1 BDBV, entered a separate Phase 1 trial in the United Kingdom in July, making it the first Bundibugyo vaccine to enter human clinical testing.

If mRNA-1469 is ultimately approved, Moderna has committed to making at least 500,000 doses available to low- and middle-income countries under access pricing as part of its agreement with CEPI.

title.rendered: The Pediatric Academy launches in Dubai to advance children’s healthcare education globally

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE— Dubai has welcomed the launch of The Pediatric Academy, a new international education institution established to improve collaboration among healthcare professionals while giving parents easier access to reliable, evidence-based information about children’s health and development.

Founded by pediatric dentist, author and international speaker Dr. Rafif Tayara, the Academy focuses on promoting a multidisciplinary approach to children’s healthcare.

Its educational programs cover pediatric dentistry, airway health, sleep-disordered breathing, oral function, early facial growth, interceptive orthodontics and myofunctional therapy.

The institution combines a global online learning platform with hands-on professional training delivered at its education center on Jumeira Street in Dubai.

Promoting multidisciplinary pediatric care

The Academy’s first programs address an area of pediatric healthcare that increasingly demands cooperation among different medical specialties.

Conditions affecting breathing, sleep, oral habits, tongue function and facial growth often influence one another, yet healthcare providers frequently assess them independently.

“Children do not experience their health in isolated specialties,” Dr. Tayara said.

“A child who breathes through the mouth, sleeps poorly or develops an abnormal oral habit may present different signs to a dentist, pediatrician, ENT specialist, speech therapist or parent. The Pediatric Academy was created to help connect those observations and encourage earlier, better-informed collaboration.”

To support this goal, the Academy offers online courses, in-person workshops, live educational events, clinical resources and professional mentorship. Its programs target pediatric dentists, general dentists, orthodontists, pediatricians, ENT specialists, dental hygienists, speech and feeding therapists, myofunctional therapists and other professionals involved in children’s health.

The Dubai training center will host workshops, professional meetings and multidisciplinary learning sessions, while the online platform enables participants worldwide to study remotely at their own pace. Selected courses will also offer continuing education credits, with accreditation details provided for each eligible program.

Resources designed for parents

Alongside professional education, The Pediatric Academy provides parents and caregivers with practical resources explaining topics such as mouth breathing, snoring, sleep quality, oral habits, early dental development and signs that may require evaluation by a qualified healthcare professional.

“Our objective is not to encourage parents to diagnose their children,” Dr. Tayara said.

“It is to help them recognize when something may deserve attention, ask better questions and find the right professional support.”

The Academy’s educational materials are available in English, Arabic, French and Dutch, reflecting its commitment to serving families and healthcare professionals across different regions.

Dubai as a global education hub

The Pediatric Academy is headquartered in Dubai and operates a European branch in Hilversum, the Netherlands.

According to Dr. Tayara, Dubai’s international population and growing role as a healthcare hub made it the ideal location for the institution.

“Dubai brings together families, clinicians and educators from an extraordinary range of backgrounds,” she said.

“It gives us the opportunity to build an institution in the Middle East that is global from its foundation—not only in where its participants come from, but also in how different cultures, disciplines and healthcare perspectives are represented.”

By combining its Dubai training center, European branch and digital learning platform, the Academy aims to connect healthcare professionals and families across geographical boundaries while encouraging knowledge exchange.

Leadership backed by international experience

Dr. Tayara brings nearly two decades of experience in pediatric dentistry, having trained and practiced across North America, the Middle East and the Gulf region.

She studied at Saint-Joseph University in Beirut and the University of Montreal before completing additional training in dental sleep medicine at Tufts University.

She also co-founded Dubai’s pediatric dental clinic JuniorDental, has delivered international lectures on airway development, early orthodontics and minimally invasive pediatric dentistry, and received the 2025 Best Pediatric Dentist Award from Mother, Baby & Child magazine.

In addition, she authored Danny and Sarah Go to Dr. Smile, a children’s book created to reduce anxiety surrounding early dental visits.
