title.rendered: Tanzania upgrades historical Kibong’oto Hospital to Tanzania Infectious Diseases Institute

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

TANZANIA—Tanzania has strengthened its capacity to prevent, diagnose and treat infectious diseases after the former Kibong’oto Infectious Diseases Hospital (KIDH) in Kilimanjaro Region was officially upgraded to the Tanzania Infectious Diseases Institute (TIDI).

The government gazetted the new status on July 24, 2026, marking a significant step in the development of specialised infectious disease services, research and training in the country.

New mandate for infectious disease control

Speaking at a press briefing, Acting TIDI Director Dr Leonard Subi said the institute’s expanded mandate would strengthen Tanzania’s ability to respond to infectious diseases while positioning the country as a regional centre for scientific research and innovation.

Dr Subi said the upgrade reflects the government’s continued investment in the health sector and its efforts to expand access to specialised healthcare.

“This achievement is among the major results of the sixth-phase government’s commitment to improving health services in the country,” he said.

He added that the institute’s transformation would support infectious disease control and strengthen scientific research and innovation, both nationally and across Africa.

Dr Subi credited President Samia Suluhu Hassan with approving the transformation, describing the decision as a new chapter for the institution and Tanzania’s healthcare system.

The president approved the hospital’s specialised organisational structure in 2022 before endorsing its elevation to institute status in line with national legislation.

Expanding healthcare, research and training

Over the years, government investment in modern infrastructure, medical equipment, technology and skilled personnel has enabled the institution to expand its specialised services.

As TIDI, the institute will continue providing specialised healthcare while conducting research and training health professionals to address current and emerging infectious disease threats.

The institute will also strengthen Tanzania’s preparedness for pandemics and public health emergencies. Its expanded role will include providing specialised treatment for highly infectious diseases, including Ebola.

In addition, TIDI will support national capacity in infectious disease management through research, professional training, knowledge sharing, networking and technical assistance to the health sector.

The institute will also enhance diagnostic, treatment and patient follow-up services for tropical infectious diseases in Tanzania and neighbouring countries.

It will achieve this through research, communication, training and consultancy services.

Institution marks 100 years

Dr Subi said the institute’s expanded mandate aligns with Tanzania’s broader healthcare reforms under the country’s Vision 2050 agenda.

“As Tanzania pursues its Vision 2050 agenda, healthcare reforms will remain central to improving people’s wellbeing. We remain committed to addressing health sector challenges under the institute’s expanded mandate,” he said.

The institution dates back to 1926, when it was established as a tuberculosis sanatorium.

It later became Kibong’oto Infectious Diseases Hospital before its transformation into the Tanzania Infectious Diseases Institute.

The elevation comes as the institution marks its centenary in 2026, 100 years after it began providing specialised care for tuberculosis patients.

title.rendered: Mayo Clinic, Stanford researchers develop blood test to predict cancer immunotherapy response

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

USA—Researchers at Mayo Clinic and Stanford Medicine have developed a blood test that can map the complex environment surrounding cancer cells, potentially providing a more accurate way to predict which patients will respond to immunotherapy.

The findings, published in Nature, mark an advance in precision oncology by allowing clinicians to assess the tumor microenvironment through a blood sample rather than an invasive tumor biopsy.

Mapping the tumor environment

Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, but only a proportion of patients benefit.

Existing biomarkers, including the number of DNA mutations in a tumor and the levels of certain proteins on cancer cells, provide limited information about how a tumor will respond.

“Until now, liquid biopsies or blood tests have focused almost entirely on tumor cells,” said Aadel Chaudhuri, M.D., Ph.D., professor of radiation oncology at Mayo Clinic and co-senior author of the study.

“For the first time, we can use a simple blood test to understand the tumor’s microenvironment.”

To develop the test, the researchers used spatial transcriptomics, a technology that shows how different cells are organized and interact within tumors.

Their analysis identified nine distinct cellular neighborhoods, known as spatial ecotypes that reflect different combinations of immune and stromal cells surrounding tumors.

The team found these ecotypes across all 17 cancer types examined.

Some occurred predominantly at the boundary between tumors and healthy tissue, while others appeared deeper within tumors.

Importantly, several ecotypes were associated with patient survival and responses to immunotherapy.

Turning tumor mapping into a blood test

The researchers then collaborated with Aaron Newman, Ph.D., associate professor of biomedical data science at Stanford Medicine, whose team developed methods to identify the cellular neighborhoods in tumor samples and an artificial intelligence (AI) framework for detecting them in blood.

The resulting liquid biopsy analyzes methylation, or chemical modifications of DNA, in cell-free DNA released by tumors into the bloodstream.

 This approach allows the test to capture information about the tumor microenvironment in addition to cancer cells.

The researchers evaluated the approach in more than 1,300 patients with several cancers, including melanoma, lung, bladder and gastric cancers.

Specific spatial ecotypes showed strong associations with treatment outcomes, with some linked to better immunotherapy responses and others associated with treatment resistance and poorer survival.

The researchers said the new approach outperformed standard biomarkers in predicting treatment outcomes.

Potential for treatment monitoring

The test could also help clinicians identify patients who are unlikely to benefit from immunotherapy before treatment begins, potentially allowing them to consider alternative therapies sooner.

Because the test requires only a blood sample, researchers also believe it could enable repeated monitoring of changes in the tumor microenvironment during treatment.

Early findings suggest that shifts in spatial ecotypes may indicate treatment response or resistance months before conventional imaging detects changes.

Although the published study focused primarily on melanoma, the researchers are investigating the approach in other cancers, including lung and bladder cancer.

They are also evaluating whether spatial ecotypes can predict responses to antibody-drug conjugate combination therapies.

Further studies will assess the test in larger patient populations and determine whether it can be incorporated into routine clinical practice.

Chaudhuri and Newman have disclosed patent filings related to liquid biopsy and cancer biomarkers, while both researchers have reported ownership or consulting interests in companies in the field.

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Kenya has strengthened efforts to reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths after the Ministry of Health and the Beginnings Fund signed a Cooperation Framework to advance equitable, high-quality maternal and newborn healthcare through nationally led reforms.

The partnership will unlock KSh10.4 billion (US$80 million) over the next five years to accelerate implementation of Kenya’s Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) Acceleration Plan and support the country’s 90-90-80-80 maternal and newborn health targets.

The programme will target 21 counties with a high burden of maternal and newborn deaths and nearly 200 high-volume health facilities.

By 2030, the interventions are expected to benefit almost six million women and newborns.

The Beginnings Fund, alongside the Gates Foundation, the Government of the United Arab Emirates and other global partners, will support the initiative.

The investment will strengthen efforts to prevent maternal and newborn deaths while helping Kenya build a more resilient and sustainable health system.

Strengthening maternal and newborn care

The partnership will complement ongoing government reforms, including the Maternal and Newborn Health Rapid Results Initiative (RRI), launched by President William Ruto under the Taifa Care programme.

The programme will strengthen health sector leadership, improve the quality of maternal and newborn care, promote innovation, support sustainable financing and reinforce accountability.

These measures will target maternal deaths, newborn mortality and stillbirths while improving the overall delivery of health services.

The investment will also expand access to lifesaving medicines, essential commodities and medical technologies.

In addition, it will support improvements to maternity and newborn facilities, expand the health workforce, strengthen emergency referral systems and accelerate the adoption of digital health solutions.

Furthermore, the programme will strengthen health information systems and support Kenya’s Universal Health Coverage agenda.

It will also align development partner investments with the government’s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA).

Government calls for coordinated action

Speaking during the signing ceremony, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said the Ministry is promoting a country-led approach to transforming the health sector.

He said development partnerships should move away from fragmented projects towards coordinated investments that strengthen government systems and deliver sustainable health outcomes.

Duale emphasized that successful implementation will require close collaboration between the national government, county governments and development partners.

He also commended the Beginnings Fund for aligning its investment with Kenya’s national health priorities.

He called for a unified approach based on one plan, one budget and one accountability framework to improve transparency, efficiency and collective responsibility.

The Cooperation Framework was signed in the presence of Principal Secretary for Medical Services Ouma Oluga, Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth, Council of Governors Chief Executive Officer Mary Mwiti and Beginnings Fund Chief Executive Officer Alice Kang’ethe.

Other attendees included World Health Organization Country Representative Neema Kimambo, Director of Family Health Bashir Issak, county government representatives, development partners, implementing agencies and senior Ministry of Health officials.

title.rendered: JOOTRH inaugurates board to guide expansion to Level 6 status

[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

KENYA—Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has conducted his first strategic meeting with the newly appointed Board of Directors of Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital (JOOTRH).

During this meeting, he outlined the government’s expectations for the facility as it assumes an expanded role as a Level 6 teaching and referral hospital.

The Board, chaired by Dr. Charles Olang’o, will oversee JOOTRH’s transformation into a major centre for specialised healthcare, medical education, research and innovation.

The expanded role is expected to strengthen referral services across Western Kenya and the wider East African region while reducing pressure on national referral hospitals.

Government outlines priorities for JOOTRH

During the meeting, Duale said the Board would play a central role in guiding the hospital’s growth and ensuring that it delivers high-quality specialised services.

He urged its members to provide visionary leadership while maintaining strong standards of integrity, accountability and corporate governance.

The Cabinet Secretary also called on the Board to manage public resources prudently and adopt a results-oriented approach to institutional development.

He emphasised the need for the hospital to strengthen service delivery while expanding its capacity to support medical training, research and innovation.

The meeting also reviewed ongoing reforms in the health sector under the Taifa Care Model.

These reforms include the Social Health Authority (SHA), which has enrolled more than 31 million Kenyans, as well as efforts to revitalise the Kenya Medical Supplies Authority (KEMSA).

According to the Ministry, KEMSA’s order fill rate has risen to 90%, indicating improved capacity to meet healthcare facilities’ demand for medicines and other medical supplies.

In addition, the Government is preparing to operationalise the National Ambulance Dispatch Centre, which will serve as Kenya’s first integrated system for coordinating emergency medical services.

Focus on specialised healthcare and UHC

Duale reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to supporting JOOTRH as it expands its role within Kenya’s healthcare system.

He said the Government would continue investing in hospital infrastructure, specialised medical services, healthcare workforce development, research and innovation.

These investments are intended to improve access to quality, affordable and people-centred healthcare while supporting the country’s pursuit of Universal Health Coverage (UHC).

The hospital’s expanded mandate will also position it to provide more specialised services closer to patients in Western Kenya and neighbouring regions.

The engagement brought together senior officials from the Ministry of Health and the hospital’s leadership.

Attendees included the Ministry’s Director of Health Sector Coordination, Dr. Ahmed Albush; the Secretary for Administration in the State Department for Medical Services, James Ntabo; and the National Eye Care Coordinator and Head of the Eye Health Section, Dr. Monicah Bitok.

title.rendered: Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center launches first global clinical trial of Silexion’s KRAS-targeting therapy for pancreatic cancer

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

ISRAEL—Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center has become the first hospital in the world to begin recruiting patients for a clinical trial evaluating an experimental therapy designed to target KRAS mutations in pancreatic cancer.

The study, launched in partnership with Israeli biotechnology company Silexion Therapeutics, marks an important step in the development of new treatment options for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

Investigational therapy targets KRAS mutations

The clinical trial will assess SIL204, an investigational treatment developed by Silexion using small interfering RNA (siRNA) technology.

The therapy is designed to suppress the activity of mutated KRAS genes inside tumor cells, potentially slowing or preventing cancer growth.

KRAS mutations occur in about 90% of pancreatic cancer cases and are widely recognized as a major driver of tumor development and disease progression.

Despite decades of research, scientists have struggled to develop therapies capable of effectively targeting these mutations, making KRAS one of the most challenging cancer targets.

Pancreatic cancer also remains one of the most aggressive malignancies because it is often diagnosed only after it has reached an advanced stage, limiting treatment options and reducing survival rates.

Trial design and patient enrollment

Under the study protocol, clinicians will administer SIL204 directly into the tumor while patients continue to receive standard systemic treatment.

Researchers aim to determine whether silencing the mutated KRAS gene can reduce tumor growth in patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer that cannot be removed through surgery.

The first phase of the study will enroll approximately 18 patients and will primarily evaluate the safety of the investigational therapy.

If successful, the trial will expand to additional medical centers across Israel, Germany, and other countries, with total enrollment expected to reach about 166 patients.

Prof. Ravit Geva, Director of the Oncology Institute and Gastrointestinal Oncology Center at Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, will lead the study at the hospital.

“Pancreatic cancer treatment is undergoing a significant transformation,” Geva said.

“We are proud to be the first center worldwide to lead this Israeli-developed approach, which combines direct intratumoral administration of the investigational treatment with systemic therapy in patients with locally advanced, unresectable disease.”

Geva added that the study brings together specialists in oncology, gastroenterology, surgery, imaging, and clinical research to ensure comprehensive patient care throughout the trial.

Company marks clinical milestone

Silexion Therapeutics, which is listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker SLXN, described the launch of patient recruitment as a major milestone following years of research, product development, and clinical preparation.

“The initiation of the study at Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center marks SIL204’s transition from years of development and clinical preparation into an active clinical program,” said Silexion Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ilan Hadar.

Hadar noted that the study is expected to evaluate whether broad and targeted silencing of KRAS mutations could provide a new therapeutic option for patients with pancreatic cancer.

SIL204 remains an investigational treatment, and its safety and effectiveness have not yet been established through clinical testing.

title.rendered: Moscow expands MosMedAI platform to scale AI radiology across 75 Russian regions

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

RUSSIA—Moscow is expanding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiology across Russia, with its medical AI systems having processed more than 16 million diagnostic studies to date.

The city is sharing its experience and technology with healthcare institutions in other regions as part of efforts to increase the use of AI in medical imaging and support faster disease detection.

MosMedAI expands nationwide

Moscow opened access to its MosMedAI platform to healthcare institutions across Russia in 2024, following a decree by Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The platform brings together computer vision services designed to analyse medical images and identify potential abnormalities.

According to the Moscow Mayor, the city has prioritised the development of AI technologies within its healthcare system in recent years and is now scaling these capabilities nationwide.

“Over the past few years, we have placed significant emphasis on developing AI technologies in Moscow’s healthcare system and have achieved substantial results,” the mayor said.

The platform provides regional healthcare organisations with access to AI services that have undergone multiple stages of testing and demonstrated their effectiveness within Moscow’s healthcare network.

These services are designed to complement physicians’ work by providing additional information during the diagnostic process.

AI supports medical image analysis

AI algorithms can identify areas of a medical image that may indicate pathology, perform specific measurements and provide additional diagnostic information to physicians.

The technology is intended to support, rather than replace, healthcare professionals by helping them identify potential diseases at an earlier stage.

In Moscow, the AI systems can currently detect as many as 14 different pathologies from a single medical image.

The technology can therefore assist radiologists in reviewing large volumes of diagnostic data while highlighting findings that may require closer examination.

The system analyzes several types of medical images, including mammograms, fluorograms, chest X-rays and computed tomography (CT) scans of the brain and thoracic organs.

MosMedAI platform reaches 75 regions

More than 2,000 medical organisations across 75 Russian regions are now connected to the MosMedAI platform.

These institutions can access 18 AI-powered services to support the analysis of diagnostic images.

Meanwhile, Moscow continues to expand the range of conditions that its AI systems can detect.

Since April, the platform has also been able to identify signs of scoliosis in spinal X-rays, adding another application to its growing portfolio of diagnostic tools.

The Center for Diagnostics and Telemedicine has so far tested 70 AI services as Moscow continues to assess and develop technologies for medical image analysis.

The centre’s work includes evaluating AI applications before they are deployed within the healthcare system, with the aim of ensuring that the tools can provide reliable support for clinical decision-making.

title.rendered: Newcastle Hospitals performs UK’s first adolescent spinal cord stimulation implantation

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UK—Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has implanted a spinal cord stimulator (SCS) in an 18-year-old patient, making him the first adolescent in the UK and one of the youngest patients globally to receive the neuromodulation therapy for pain management.

Ralph Seed, from Washington in Tyne and Wear, has lived with severe foot pain caused by complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) for five years.

The rare condition became so debilitating that he could no longer walk or put weight on his foot.

At one point, the severity of his pain led him to ask doctors whether amputation was an option.

However, conventional treatments, including painkillers and physiotherapy, failed to provide adequate relief.

As a result, surgeons at Newcastle Hospitals offered Seed the opportunity to receive Medtronic’s Inceptiv SCS system.

 Until then, clinicians in the UK had used SCS implants only in adults.

Closed-loop technology targets pain signals

Inceptiv uses closed-loop technology to monitor and adjust stimulation in response to changes in the spinal cord.

The system delivers mild electrical impulses that interfere with pain signals before they reach the brain, potentially providing more responsive pain control.

Medtronic received a CE mark for Inceptiv in August 2023, followed by clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in April 2024.

Because Seed was the youngest person in the UK to undergo an SCS implantation, his medical team first performed an exploratory procedure.

During this initial stage, clinicians inserted the device’s leads into his lower back to stimulate the spinal cord and assess his response before proceeding with the full implantation.

Immediate improvement after surgery

Dr Sachin Rastogi, consultant anaesthetist, and Akbar Hussain, consultant neurosurgeon and functional neurosurgeon, performed the procedure at the Royal Victoria Infirmary, part of the Newcastle Hospitals group.

According to the clinical team, Seed experienced an immediate and dramatic reduction in pain when they activated the device following surgery.

“The results were immediate and unprecedented for a device like this. Seeing the impact of being pain-free for Ralph is simply one of the most moving things I have experienced in my career,” said Dr Rastogi.

He added that the closed-loop SCS approach had not previously been used in the UK for an adolescent with this type of pain.

He suggested that Seed’s young and adaptable nervous system may have contributed to his strong response to the treatment.

Growing role of spinal cord stimulation

SCS is a form of neuromodulation used to treat chronic and severe nerve pain affecting the trunk, arms or legs when conventional treatments have failed.

The technology is increasingly being used as clinicians explore alternatives for patients who do not respond adequately to standard pain management approaches.

Meanwhile, a recent GlobalData report forecasts that the North American SCS market will reach US$3.5 billion by 2033.

The market has also attracted growing attention from major medical technology companies.

At the North American Neuromodulation Society (NANS) annual meeting in January, Boston Scientific presented data highlighting the benefits of its SCS therapies.

Abbott also presented findings from its SCS portfolio, including a retrospective analysis of more than 16,000 patients.

The analysis found that the company’s SCS therapy was associated with an average 75% reduction in short- and long-term pain-related healthcare visits after five years of treatment.

title.rendered: Sidra Medicine administers Novartis’ Itvisma gene therapy to Qatar’s first SMA patient

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||61px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

QATAR—Sidra Medicine, a member of Qatar Foundation, has administered Itvisma (onasemnogene abeparvovec), a one-time gene replacement therapy, to a 13-year-old patient with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), becoming the first hospital in Qatar to deliver the treatment.

The milestone also makes Qatar the third country worldwide to administer Itvisma and marks a significant step in the country’s precision medicine and rare disease care efforts.

Prof. Ibrahim Janahi, Chief Medical Officer at Sidra Medicine, said the treatment represented an important milestone for the hospital and the future of rare disease care in Qatar.

He added that the achievement demonstrates the value of combining multidisciplinary expertise, precision medicine, and advanced interventional radiology to improve outcomes for patients with complex genetic conditions.

According to Janahi, Sidra Medicine aims to ensure eligible patients and their families can access advanced therapies closer to home through coordinated care pathways that provide support before, during, and after treatment.

Targeting the genetic cause of SMA

SMA is a rare genetic neuromuscular disorder caused by a missing or non-functional survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.

As a result, the body produces insufficient levels of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein, which is essential for motor neuron survival and normal muscle function.

Itvisma is designed to address the underlying cause of SMA by delivering a functional copy of the human SMN1 gene through a single intrathecal injection.

Patients undergo comprehensive clinical and genetic assessments to determine their eligibility for treatment.

Prof. Tawfeg Ben Omran, Division Chief of Genetics and Genomic Medicine at Sidra Medicine, said gene therapy is changing the treatment landscape for SMA by shifting care from symptom management towards addressing the disease at its genetic source.

He added that comprehensive genetic evaluation, careful patient selection, and long-term multidisciplinary follow-up are essential to achieving the best possible outcomes.

Multidisciplinary approach

The treatment followed months of preparation involving specialists in genetics and genomic medicine, interventional radiology, neurology, pharmacy, anesthesiology, pediatric intensive care, pulmonology, physiotherapy and rehabilitation, nursing, endocrinology, and orthopedic spine services.

The therapy was administered through a single intrathecal injection in the interventional radiology unit.

The image-guided approach enabled clinicians to visualize the procedure in real time, navigate complex anatomy, and accurately position the needle for delivery into the spinal canal.

Dr. Walid Mubarak, Senior Attending Physician in Interventional Radiology at Sidra Medicine, said detailed planning and precise delivery are critical when administering a one-time intrathecal therapy.

He added that advanced imaging capabilities enable clinicians to perform the procedure accurately while maintaining patient safety.

Expanding access to gene therapy

Mohammed Ezz Eldin, Head of the GCC Cluster at Novartis, said the milestone highlights the importance of collaboration between healthcare providers and industry partners in expanding access to innovative treatments for patients with significant unmet needs.

For Khalid and his family, the treatment marks the culmination of years of seeking specialist care and exploring advances in SMA treatment.

His mother said receiving the therapy in Qatar had been a dream come true after the family travelled internationally in search of treatment options.

Khalid, who attends Qatar Academy Sidra, said he was grateful to the healthcare teams that supported him and hoped to continue his studies and become a doctor.

Itvisma is registered with Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health, allowing eligible patients to access the therapy locally following specialist assessment.

Khalid will continue receiving follow-up care at Sidra Medicine, including laboratory monitoring, corticosteroid management, and assessments of motor function, respiratory health, mobility, rehabilitation goals, and overall well-being.

title.rendered: Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi debuts Middle East’s first robotically assisted bronchoscopy platform

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||61px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE— Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi has introduced the Middle East’s first robotically assisted bronchoscopy technology, enabling physicians to access and biopsy some of the smallest and most difficult-to-reach lung nodules.

These nodules can be among the earliest visible signs of lung cancer, and the technology is designed to support more accurate diagnosis at an earlier stage without the need for open surgery.

The hospital has introduced the MONARCH™ platform, which allows physicians to navigate a flexible endoscope deep into the lungs with greater stability, control and precision.

The system enables clinicians to target small and hard-to-reach nodules in real time, supporting tissue biopsy and more accurate diagnosis.

By improving access to areas of the lungs that can be challenging to reach using conventional bronchoscopy, the technology could help physicians identify lung cancer and other lung diseases earlier.

Earlier diagnosis can, in turn, give clinicians more opportunities to intervene at the appropriate time and develop targeted treatment strategies based on each patient’s condition.

Minimally invasive approach

The robotically assisted bronchoscopy procedure is performed under general anaesthesia and typically takes between 30 and 75 minutes.

Because the approach is minimally invasive, patients can avoid the need for open surgery to access certain lung nodules.

The technology is intended to support a safer and less invasive diagnostic experience while improving the accuracy and speed of diagnosis.

By enabling physicians to reach smaller lesions with greater precision, the platform could also help clinicians make more informed treatment decisions and improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

Supporting Abu Dhabi’s healthcare transformation

The introduction of the technology has received support from the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, which is advancing the adoption of innovative healthcare technologies that can deliver tangible benefits for patients.

The initiative also aligns with Abu Dhabi’s broader vision of developing a proactive healthcare ecosystem that places greater emphasis on prediction, early detection and prevention.

By integrating advanced technologies into clinical care, healthcare providers can strengthen their ability to identify diseases earlier and deliver more personalised interventions.

Dr. Georges-Pascal Haber, Chief Executive Officer at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, said the introduction of robotically assisted bronchoscopy demonstrates the hospital’s commitment to bringing transformative, precision-led technologies to the Middle East.

He added that investing in advanced, technology-enabled solutions is helping the hospital redefine the patient experience by supporting safer, less invasive care while enhancing diagnostic accuracy.

Potential for future cancer treatment

Dr. Zaid Zoumot, Division Chair of Pulmonary Medicine at the Integrated Hospital Care Institute at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, described robotically assisted bronchoscopy as a significant advancement in the detection and diagnosis of lung disease.

He said the technology enables physicians to precisely access and biopsy some of the smallest and most difficult-to-reach lung nodules.

This capability could support earlier diagnosis of lung cancer, when the disease may be more amenable to treatment and patients may have better outcomes.

Looking ahead, the technology could also support the development of additional minimally invasive applications.

These may include robotic surgical interventions for cancer and the treatment of detected lung nodules using techniques such as ablation, heat or cold therapy.

title.rendered: Sheba Medical Center collaborates with OpenAI to increase access to healthcare AI models

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||61px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

ISRAEL— Sheba Medical Center, through its ARC innovation center, has entered into a strategic partnership with OpenAI to give physicians at the country’s largest hospital access to the company’s healthcare-focused artificial intelligence (AI) models.

The agreement makes Sheba the first hospital outside the United States to join OpenAI’s healthcare program and gain access to its dedicated suite of medical AI tools.

The partnership was signed with Nate Gross, OpenAI’s head of health, according to Calcalist.

A delegation from Sheba is also expected to visit OpenAI’s headquarters in August for meetings with senior executives.

The collaboration includes access to OpenAI’s healthcare models, including ChatGPT Health, which the company introduced in January and has made available to a limited number of US hospitals.

The models are designed to support clinicians by helping them evaluate medical information, make decisions and develop treatment plans based on current clinical research.

OpenAI has designed the system with encryption and security measures intended to meet the requirements of healthcare organizations.

Under the agreement, Sheba physicians will receive early access to new healthcare models before their wider release, while the partnership will also expand research collaboration between the two organizations.

Clinical applications and research collaboration

As part of the agreement, dedicated teams at Sheba will contribute to product development and gain early insights into new models while OpenAI develops them.

 The teams will also participate in OpenAI healthcare events and create internal applications optimized for the platform.

In addition, Sheba plans to incorporate its clinical protocols, treatment pathways and institutional guidelines into OpenAI’s models.

This integration could enable the system to provide responses aligned with the hospital’s approved standards and, eventually, support recommendations tailored to Israeli clinical practice.

In daily clinical and research settings, physicians and researchers will be able to submit patient case descriptions and receive responses that include relevant medical literature, supporting studies, journal references, and publication dates.

These citations will allow clinicians to independently review and verify the evidence supporting the information provided by the AI system.

The technology is also expected to support administrative and operational tasks.

By assisting with documentation and other routine workflows, the platform could help reduce the administrative workload for healthcare professionals and improve efficiency across the hospital.

Sheba expands its AI innovation portfolio

The partnership builds on Sheba’s expanding use of AI technologies through its ARC innovation center.

The portfolio includes solutions developed by Aidoc, which uses AI to analyze medical images and help accelerate the diagnosis of critical conditions.

It also includes SmartER, an emergency department platform that automatically documents and summarizes patient encounters.

Sheba established ARC in 2019 under the leadership of Director General Prof. Yitshak Kreiss and Chief Transformation and Innovation Officer Dr. Eyal Zimlichman.

 The center focuses on accelerating digital healthcare innovation by enabling startups to test emerging technologies within the hospital.

ARC also develops strategic partnerships with healthcare institutions worldwide and operates an investment platform in collaboration with TriVentures.

“The healthcare system is one of the fields where artificial intelligence can have the greatest impact,” OpenAI said in a statement.

“We are excited to collaborate with Sheba to make advanced AI capabilities available to doctors, researchers, and healthcare professionals.”

title.rendered: Aster Clinics UAE to expand network to more than 100 facilities by 2030

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE — Aster Clinics UAE, the largest private primary care network under Aster DM Healthcare’s GCC group, plans to expand its network from 85 to more than 100 facilities across the UAE by 2030, supported by an investment commitment of AED 100 million (US$27.2 million).

The expansion will combine new clinics with the enlargement of existing facilities and is expected to increase Aster Clinics’ workforce to 4,100 employees across the UAE.

The new and expanded facilities will add specialty centres, enhance in-clinic diagnostic services, and integrate digital and smart healthcare solutions through myAster.

The network will also expand homecare and personalised care services.

The growth follows a 15% increase in annual patient visits across Aster Clinics over the past year, reflecting rising demand for accessible primary healthcare services.

Strengthening clinical services

Alongside expanding its geographical footprint, Aster Clinics is strengthening its clinical capabilities through specialty-led models.

The network plans to scale diabetes care using a “clinic within a clinic” approach, enabling patients to access integrated and convenient services for chronic disease management.

Aster Clinics is also expanding its orthopaedic and physiotherapy services to provide comprehensive care for bone and joint conditions.

These initiatives form part of the organisation’s broader strategy to deliver integrated, community-based healthcare across the UAE.

Outpatient services account for more than 70% of healthcare interactions in the UAE, highlighting the importance of primary care networks as the first point of contact for patients.

Aster’s extensive clinic network is therefore positioned to meet growing demand for accessible healthcare closer to where people live and work.

Aster Clinics UAE currently operates 85 clinics across the Emirates, supported by 13 Access Clinics.

The group also operates two clinics in Bahrain, while its wider GCC network comprises more than 100 clinics.

Expanding specialised and personalised care

Alisha Moopen, Managing Director and Group CEO of Aster DM Healthcare, said the UAE remains a cornerstone of the group’s long-term strategy, supported by the country’s healthcare ecosystem and vision for integrated care delivery.

She added that Aster’s growth strategy focuses on building a sustainable healthcare model that combines clinical excellence, digital innovation, and community-based services.

Recent developments include the launch of Aster Clinic Jaddaf, which has expanded access to healthcare in a growing residential area.

Specialised facilities, including the Aster Diabetes 360 Care Clinic and Aster Children’s Clinic in Dubai Silicon Oasis, further support the group’s focus on chronic disease management, family healthcare, and personalised services.

The group is also expanding the Aster Orthopaedic Clinic in Qusais and strengthening women’s health services at Aster Clinic Gardens, supported by enhanced radiology capabilities.

Digital and home-based healthcare

Dr Sherbaz Bichu, CEO of Aster Hospitals & Clinics (UAE, Bahrain & Oman), said the expansion reflects the organisation’s commitment to making quality healthcare more accessible and affordable.

Aster is also aligning its growth with the UAE’s increasing focus on preventive and digitally enabled healthcare.

Its myAster platform supports teleconsultations and continuity of care, while Aster @Home provides consultations, diagnostics, and nursing services at patients’ homes, hotels, or offices.

The group is expanding its wellness portfolio with services such as intravenous therapies and plans to introduce peptide-based treatments as part of its focus on preventive and personalised care.

 Programmes including Care for Her, a women’s health and wellness initiative, and Age Well with Aster, a senior care programme, also address growing demand for specialised services.

Further network expansion

Aster Clinics UAE plans to continue investing in capacity expansion, express clinics in high-density locations, and Neubridge Diagnostics to strengthen diagnostic services across its healthcare ecosystem.

The network will prioritise densely populated residential corridors and emerging communities, responding to population growth and increasing demand for neighbourhood-based healthcare accessible within 10 to 15 minutes.

Manish Jain, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of Aster & Access Clinics UAE and Bahrain, said the group’s expansion strategy is structured around community needs.

He added that Aster is focused not only on opening new facilities but also on strengthening services within its existing network to improve both accessibility and clinical value for patients.

title.rendered: Mayo Clinic expands Middle East footprint with opening of Riyadh Representative Office

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

SAUDI ARABIA— Mayo Clinic has opened a new patient representative office in Riyadh to help patients, families, healthcare providers, insurers and referring physicians in the region access its specialised medical services.

The new office strengthens Mayo Clinic’s presence in the Middle East and provides a direct link between patients in Saudi Arabia and its medical campuses in the US and UK.

It joins 20 other Mayo Clinic representative offices across Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and Asia, including the organisation’s established regional hub in Dubai Healthcare City.

Supporting patients and families

Staff at the Riyadh office speak Arabic and English and assist patients seeking appointments at Mayo Clinic locations in Rochester, Minnesota; Phoenix and Scottsdale, Arizona; Jacksonville, Florida; and Mayo Clinic Healthcare in London.

In addition, the office helps patients and their families navigate the administrative aspects of seeking treatment abroad.

This support includes coordinating appointments, arranging travel and accommodation, addressing billing and insurance matters, and providing general information about Mayo Clinic.

The services come at no cost to patients, although the office does not provide medical care.

“Mayo Clinic welcomes patients from around the world who need specialised care for serious and complex medical conditions,” said Omar Ghanem, MD, Mayo Clinic’s medical director for the Middle East and chair of the Division of Metabolic and Abdominal Wall Reconstructive Surgery in Rochester.

“The Riyadh office staff helps patients in the region connect with Mayo Clinic and navigate every stage of the process, from exploring appointments to planning travel and housing,” he added.

Connecting regional healthcare providers

The office also supports healthcare providers, payers and other organisations seeking to connect with Mayo Clinic.

Mayo Clinic accepts appointment requests directly from patients as well as referrals from physicians.

To facilitate communication, the healthcare provider makes interpreters available at no cost for patients whose primary language is not English.

Its care teams also coordinate services across specialties to provide patients with a seamless experience.

This approach includes scheduling consultations, diagnostic tests and procedures close to one another where possible, while one personal physician coordinates the patient’s care.

Mayo Clinic also facilitates communication between its teams and patients’ healthcare providers in their home countries.

Supporting GCC healthcare transformation

The Riyadh office also reflects growing demand for cross-border coordination of complex medical care in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region.

Through the office, Mayo Clinic aims to simplify administrative, language and travel arrangements for patients seeking advanced treatment for serious or rare conditions.

At the same time, the organisation intends to complement healthcare transformation programmes across the GCC by supporting international collaboration between physicians and promoting knowledge sharing.

 The office is located at 3228 Imam Saud Ibn Faisal Road, Al Malqa District, Riyadh.

Mayo Clinic is ranked the world’s best hospital by Newsweek and has more top-ranked specialties than any other US hospital, according to U.S. News & World Report.

title.rendered: Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi implants first wireless heart sensor for remote heart failure monitoring

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE—Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi has become the first hospital in Abu Dhabi to implant an advanced heart-monitoring sensor designed to detect early signs of worsening chronic heart failure.

The minimally invasive technology enables doctors to monitor patients remotely and identify changes in their condition before symptoms become severe.

The system sends data directly to the patient’s care team, allowing clinicians to intervene earlier, adjust treatment, and provide more personalised care without requiring patients to visit the hospital.

Wireless sensor enables remote monitoring

The procedure involves implanting a tiny wireless sensor in the pulmonary artery, a major blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the lungs.

The device continuously measures pulmonary artery pressure and securely transmits the data to the patient’s healthcare team.

By monitoring changes in pressure over time, physicians can identify early warning signs of worsening heart failure that may not yet be apparent through symptoms alone.

This approach allows clinicians to respond more quickly to changes in a patient’s condition, including by adjusting medications and other aspects of treatment.

The hospital said the technology strengthens its remote patient monitoring capabilities and supports a more proactive approach to heart failure management.

It also enables patients to receive continuous oversight while living away from the hospital.

Dr Georges-Pascal Haber, Chief Executive Officer at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, said the technology would change how clinicians manage patients with chronic heart failure.

“Instead of waiting for symptoms to worsen and require hospitalization, we can now monitor patients proactively and intervene earlier,” he said.

“This reflects our broader commitment to delivering the most advanced solutions of preventive, patient-centered healthcare.”

Dr Nadya Almatrooshi, Staff Physician in Cardiovascular Medicine at the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, said continuous remote monitoring could give patients greater confidence in managing their condition.

“Patients often report improved symptom control, better exercise tolerance, and greater peace of mind knowing their care team is monitoring them closely,” she said.

First patients receive the implant

The implantable monitoring device is intended for patients with moderate to severe heart failure who are receiving guideline-directed medical therapy and have experienced at least one heart failure-related hospitalisation in the previous 12 months.

The first two patients to undergo the procedure at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi were Emirati nationals aged 62 and 79.

Both had a history of repeated hospital admissions caused by worsening heart failure, including symptoms such as shortness of breath and fluid build-up.

Clinicians perform the procedure in the hospital’s cardiac catheterisation laboratory, which is accredited by the American College of Cardiology.

The procedure typically takes one to two hours and uses local anaesthesia and mild sedation.

Patients are generally monitored for four to 24 hours following implantation, although some can return home on the same day.

Most resume normal activities within one to two days, with only minor temporary restrictions.

Expanding advanced cardiac care

Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi said the introduction of the technology forms part of its efforts to advance cardiovascular care in the UAE through innovative monitoring and treatment solutions.

The hospital has been designated a Center of Excellence for adult cardiac surgery by the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi and was ranked the number one hospital in the Middle East for cardiology in Newsweek’s Best Specialized Hospitals Middle East 2026 rankings.

In 2025, it also received Center of Excellence designation for cardiac catheterization procedures from the American College of Cardiology.

As the first hospital in Abu Dhabi to introduce the implantable monitoring technology, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi is expanding access to advanced heart failure management and enabling patients to receive specialized care closer to home.

title.rendered: EHS introduces twice-yearly schizophrenia treatment BYANNLI at Al Amal Psychiatric Hospital

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}”]

UAE—Emirates Health Services (EHS) has announced the introduction of BYANNLI, developed by Johnson & Johnson, for patients with schizophrenia at Al Amal Psychiatric Hospital, one of its affiliated facilities.

The hospital is the first government healthcare facility in the UAE to offer the long-acting treatment, which can be administered once every six months.

The extended dosing schedule represents a significant development in schizophrenia care, potentially reducing the frequency of treatment administration while supporting continuity of care.

His Excellency Dr. Essam Al Zarooni, Executive Director of the Clinical Services Sector at EHS, said the introduction of BYANNLI demonstrates the organisation’s commitment to providing patients with access to internationally approved treatment options.

He added that the move supports the UAE’s efforts to advance mental health services in line with global best practices.

According to Dr. Al Zarooni, the treatment also marks an important step in developing mental healthcare services that prioritise patients’ needs, quality of life and long-term health outcomes.

By expanding access to longer-acting treatment options, EHS aims to provide more sustainable care while improving the overall patient experience.

Supporting treatment continuity

Dr. Noor Almheiri, Director of the Mental Health Department at EHS, said maintaining treatment continuity remains a major challenge in managing chronic mental health conditions.

She explained that BYANNLI offers an advanced treatment option that could support continuity of care, reduce the risk of relapse and promote greater psychological and social stability among patients.

She added that improving treatment continuity and ensuring regular follow-up could have positive effects not only on patients but also on their families and caregivers.

EHS considers the introduction of BYANNLI an important addition to its mental health services as it continues to develop care models based on international best practices.

Improving long-term schizophrenia care

The introduction of the treatment comes amid rapid advances in mental healthcare.

Its six-month dosing schedule is designed to support sustained symptom control while reducing the need for frequent treatment administration.

As a result, the approach could help strengthen treatment adherence, facilitate consistent medical follow-up and contribute to more efficient use of healthcare resources.

Schizophrenia is a chronic and complex mental health disorder that can significantly affect patients, their families and caregivers when inadequately managed.

Therefore, continuity and sustainability of treatment remain important elements of care, particularly in efforts to reduce relapse, support psychological and family stability and improve quality of life.

EHS said these priorities align with the objectives of the UAE’s Year of Family and its National Strategy for Wellbeing 2031.

Hospital reports improved treatment outcomes

Al Amal Psychiatric Hospital has reported positive outcomes from its use of long-acting treatments among patients with chronic mental health disorders.

According to EHS, these treatments have helped reduce patient readmission rates to healthcare facilities to below 1%, while treatment plan adherence has reached 93%.

The hospital also reported notable improvements in psychiatric symptoms among 93% of patients receiving these treatments.

EHS attributed these outcomes to the quality of care provided at the facility and the effectiveness of its treatment models.

By introducing BYANNLI within the government healthcare sector, EHS is expanding its range of mental health treatment options while continuing to focus on integrated, proactive and patient-centred care.

 The initiative also reflects the organisation’s emphasis on innovation, quality and sustainable healthcare as the UAE advances its ambition to develop a world-class healthcare system.

title.rendered: Sidra Medicine research shows maternal diet shapes child health through epigenetics

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

QATAR—Sidra Medicine, a member of the Qatar Foundation, is advancing research into precision nutrition, with new studies showing how a mother’s diet during pregnancy may affect pregnancy outcomes and influence her child’s long-term health.

Researchers at Sidra Medicine’s Precision Nutrition Laboratory have published two studies examining how maternal nutrition affects fetal development through epigenetic changes.

These biological processes influence how genes function without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

Dr Annalisa Terranegra, Head of the Precision Nutrition Laboratory in the Translational Medicine Department at Sidra Medicine, said nutrition is among the earliest and most influential factors affecting human health.

She added that the research shows how a mother’s diet during pregnancy can leave measurable biological signatures that affect fetal development and potentially influence health throughout life.

Understanding these mechanisms, she said, could support personalised nutritional recommendations to reduce pregnancy complications and promote healthier outcomes for children.

Maternal diet linked to preterm birth

The first study, published in npj Science of Food, examined the relationship between maternal nutrition and preterm birth.

Researchers found that women who delivered prematurely consumed significantly lower amounts of protein, vitamins and essential minerals than those who carried their pregnancies to term.

The researchers also identified distinct epigenetic changes in the placenta and umbilical cord blood, particularly in genes involved in fetal development and immune function.

The findings suggest that inadequate protein intake during pregnancy may contribute to biological changes associated with a higher risk of preterm birth and could eventually help identify pregnancies at risk earlier.

Nutrition and gestational diabetes

The second study, published in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, focused on gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), a common pregnancy complication worldwide.

Researchers found that women diagnosed with GDM consumed higher amounts of saturated fat and lower levels of vitamin D and folate than women with healthy pregnancies.

The study also identified widespread epigenetic changes in genes involved in insulin regulation and glucose metabolism, including ZFP57.

These findings indicate that maternal dietary patterns may influence a child’s future metabolic health and potentially affect susceptibility to chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes.

The research also highlights the potential benefits of early nutritional assessments and targeted dietary interventions for women at risk of GDM.

Expanding precision nutrition research

Sidra Medicine is also investigating how the type and quality of dietary fats consumed during pregnancy may affect early brain development and the future risk of neurodevelopmental conditions, including autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Terranegra said the studies add to growing evidence supporting precision nutrition as an important component of maternal and child healthcare.

She noted that Sidra Medicine is expanding research into nutritional genomics, epigenetics and the microbiome to develop personalised approaches that improve pregnancy outcomes and promote healthier future generations.

Dr Ibrahim Mamoun Ibrahim, Senior Attending Physician, Endocrinology, and Lead for Diabetes in Pregnancy at Sidra Medicine, said GDM is one of the most common pregnancy complications but can be managed more effectively when women receive timely support.

He added that nutrition should be considered an integral part of medical care during pregnancy and that combining research with personalised nutritional guidance could improve pregnancy outcomes while reducing future metabolic disease risks.

The studies form part of Sidra Medicine’s broader Precision Nutrition initiative, which integrates research, clinical expertise and personalised care to develop evidence-based nutritional strategies for maternal and child health.

UAE—DataFlow Group, a global provider of Primary Source Verification (PSV) and credential verification services, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Saudi German Health (SGH), one of the largest private healthcare networks in the Arab world, to strengthen the verification of healthcare professionals in the UAE.

The agreement was signed during a ceremony at Saudi German Hospital in Dubai and establishes DataFlow as the designated PSV partner for healthcare practitioners referred by SGH.

The partnership aims to support the healthcare network in verifying practitioners’ qualifications and meeting the requirements of UAE health regulators.

Verification and licensing support

Under the agreement, SGH-referred healthcare practitioners will have access to DataFlow’s range of services, including Premium PSV, VIP Assist, Document Concierge, licensing and credentialing support, digital footprint checks and Prometric nursing exam training.

The partnership will also support eligible UAE Golden Visa applications and provide DataFlow employees with access to a dedicated VIP Service Desk at Saudi German Health facilities.

By conducting primary source checks, the collaboration will help SGH verify the authenticity of healthcare practitioners’ qualifications before they begin working within its facilities.

The organizations said the process will support patient safety and strengthen public confidence in the qualifications of healthcare professionals providing care across SGH’s hospitals and clinics in the UAE.

Commenting on the agreement, Sunil Kumar, Chief Executive Officer of DataFlow Group, said verified credentials form the foundation of safe and high-quality healthcare.

He added that the MOU reflects a shared commitment to ensuring that healthcare practitioners entering clinical environments undergo thorough and efficient verification.

Kumar said DataFlow was proud to bring its technology and global verification network to support SGH’s mission of delivering high-quality healthcare.

Supporting faster practitioner onboarding

Saudi German Health operates a growing network of medical centers across the Middle East and has maintained a focus on the quality and regulatory compliance of its clinical workforce.

The agreement is expected to help the healthcare provider accelerate practitioner onboarding while maintaining regulatory requirements.

Abdelhakim Farag Gamaleldin, Group HR Director at Saudi German Health LLC, said healthcare practitioners remain central to the organization’s operations and that accurate and timely credential verification is essential to maintaining patient trust.

He added that the partnership with DataFlow provides SGH with access to verification infrastructure that can help the organization process practitioner credentials efficiently while meeting the expectations of patients and healthcare regulators.

The MOU will remain in effect for an initial 12-month period, with the option for renewal through mutual agreement.

DataFlow will also assign a dedicated point of contact to SGH and provide access to its client portal, enabling the healthcare provider to track application progress and monitor key performance indicators in real time.

title.rendered: UHAS Mega-Lab construction resumes under President Mahama’s Reset Agenda

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

GHANA—Construction has resumed on a multipurpose laboratory complex at the University of Health and Allied Sciences (UHAS) Sokode Campus, in a move aligned with President John Dramani Mahama’s “Reset Agenda” and its focus on expanding access to quality education and practical skills.

The renewed work aims to complete the university’s 5,300-square-metre Laboratory Complex, a project that began in 2014 but stalled for several years.

Its revival is expected to address a major infrastructure gap in medical education while supporting efforts to equip Ghanaian students with practical skills relevant to the healthcare sector.

Facility to expand hands-on medical training

Once completed, the facility will become the largest laboratory complex of its kind in Ghana and the wider sub-region.

The five-block development will accommodate more than 1,200 students and staff and will include specialised research, anatomy, and radiology simulation laboratories.

The expanded infrastructure will enable UHAS to move beyond predominantly theoretical instruction by giving students greater access to practical, hands-on training.

In addition, advanced simulation equipment will allow learners to develop technical skills in a controlled environment before entering clinical and professional settings.

The investment is expected to strengthen the university’s capacity to produce graduates who can transition more effectively into the healthcare workforce, while also improving opportunities for research and innovation.

Laboratory services to generate additional revenue

Beyond its educational role, the complex is expected to contribute to the university’s financial sustainability.

UHAS plans to use the facility to provide diagnostic, toxicology, and research services to hospitals, private companies, and other institutions across Ghana.

Revenue generated through these services could provide additional Internally Generated Funds (IGF) to support the operation and maintenance of the facility and its specialised equipment.

The approach is intended to reduce reliance on public funding for the upkeep of the university’s high-technology infrastructure.

Regional access and economic opportunities

The laboratory complex is also expected to strengthen UHAS’s regional role and attract students and researchers from other parts of West Africa.

Located in the Volta Region, which shares borders with Togo and is connected to the wider West African region, the university is positioned to serve an increasingly international student population.

At the same time, road infrastructure improvements are expected to make Ho and surrounding areas more accessible, potentially easing travel for students, researchers, healthcare professionals, and other visitors.

As activity around the university increases, demand for accommodation, transportation, retail, and other services could also rise.

Local businesses and communities around Ho and towns hosting UHAS satellite campuses are therefore expected to benefit from increased economic activity linked to education, research, healthcare services, and student spending.

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi Stem Cells Centre discovers new potential treatment target for Huntington’s disease

content.rendered:
[et_pb_section fb_built=”1″ _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_row _builder_version=”4.27.5″ _module_preset=”default” custom_margin=”6px|auto||auto||” custom_padding=”15px|||41px||” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_column type=”4_4″ _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”][et_pb_text _builder_version=”4.27.4″ _module_preset=”default” global_colors_info=”{}” theme_builder_area=”post_content”]

UAE— The Abu Dhabi Stem Cells Centre (ADSCC) has reported a scientific breakthrough in Huntington’s disease research after identifying a previously unrecognised mechanism that could provide a new target for developing treatments for the inherited neurological disorder.

The findings, generated using patient-derived stem cells and advanced brain models, could support the development of targeted therapies for Huntington’s disease, which progressively damages movement, cognitive function and behavioural control.

 Despite decades of research, available treatments remain limited and do not address the underlying cause of the disease.

Study identifies role of astrocytes

To investigate the mechanisms driving the disease, ADSCC researchers collected skin and blood cells from patients at different stages of Huntington’s disease, including children and adults.

They reprogrammed the cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and then differentiated them into brain tissue containing neurons and astrocytes.

This approach enabled the team to study disease processes in a patient-specific laboratory environment.

 The research showed that disease progression may involve not only neurons but also astrocytes, specialised support cells that play a critical role in maintaining healthy brain function.

Specifically, researchers found that mutant huntingtin protein prevents astrocytes from developing and maintaining their internal structural framework.

Further analysis showed that the abnormal protein disrupts three molecular pathways that regulate the production of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), a structural protein essential for normal astrocyte function.

Potential therapeutic approach

The team subsequently introduced mutant huntingtin protein into healthy cells and reproduced the cellular abnormalities observed in patients.

Researchers then tested three therapeutic compounds that can restore the disrupted molecular pathways.

Following treatment, the affected astrocytes recovered their normal structure and function. The researchers also validated the findings using genetically engineered fruit fly models of Huntington’s disease.

Untreated flies showed impaired movement and reduced climbing ability, whereas treated flies demonstrated significant improvements in motor function.

 These results provided preclinical evidence supporting further investigation of the therapeutic approach.

The researchers said the patient-derived stem cell platform could also advance research into other inherited neurological and genetic disorders, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), leukodystrophies, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, Alexander disease and sickle cell disease.

Researchers highlight potential for clinical translation

Dr Fatima Al Kaabi, Consultant Haematologist and Bone Marrow Transplanter, Executive Director of the Abu Dhabi Bone Marrow Transplant Programme at ADSCC and Board Member of ADSCC/Yas Clinic Group, said the research reflects the centre’s commitment to advancing scientific discovery and translating research into potential therapies.

Professor Angelo L. Vescovi, Professor of Cell Biology and lead researcher, said Huntington’s disease research had focused primarily on neurons for more than three decades.

However, the study indicates that astrocytes may play a more significant role in disease progression than previously recognised.

He added that identifying the molecular mechanisms underlying astrocyte dysfunction could provide a new biological target for future Huntington’s disease therapies.

 One of the compounds tested is already undergoing Phase III clinical trials for another indication, potentially supporting faster clinical development if subsequent research confirms its safety and effectiveness in Huntington’s disease.

The findings are expected to be published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.
